7932216d020c6df922bf4144.title_original: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues
7932216d020c6df922bf4144.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-trained language models fabricate citations at high rates. We ask whether that is reward hacking: scoring well on a proxy for scholarship while doing worse on what it stands for. We ran four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions (US federal case law, computationally adjacent scientific literature, and medical literature) across twelve open-weights checkpoints covering four post-training stages of three model families, then refit on fifteen. The clearest result holds the weights fixed and changes only the prompt. Asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones: a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains. A length-matched control separates the citation cue from a demand for a longer answer, so the effect is specific to citations, not verbosity. Post-training also raises fabrication overall, from 4.8% to 56.7%, but our registered prediction that it would rise most where fabrication is most tempting did not hold. A preference model trained only on surface citation features prefers post-trained output 86% of the time, and holding citation count fixed shows it rewards quantity. Our answer: possibly, but not proven. Post-trained models produce fabricated citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator that counts sources without checking them would prefer their out

7f0b2bbc1c677f8cec314998.title_original: Urban functional knowledge transfer through global representations amid uneven data
7f0b2bbc1c677f8cec314998.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Urban functional observations are unevenly distributed worldwide, limiting analysis of how places are organised and used. AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) provides a globally consistent physical representation. Whether this representation can support transfer of functional knowledge to locations with sparse or absent functional observations, and what governs transfer, remain unclear. We introduce POI-aligned Urban Embedding (PURE), which learns physical-functional relationships between POI-derived semantics and AEF. Across five urban analysis tasks covering 142 countries and territories, PURE increases mean $R^2$ from 0.792 to 0.830, with gains across widely different levels of POI availability. When target-city POIs are excluded, country-level alignment retains 87.9% of its performance gain. Cross-country experiments show that transfer is selective rather than universal, with larger gains between physically similar and geographically closer contexts, particularly among pairs within the same continent. Our findings reveal spatially structured urban functional knowledge transfer, offering a route to reduce reliance on dense local observations.

12c9e8e7c2237b07a603b178.title_original: Large language models underrepresent malice and overreport virtue
12c9e8e7c2237b07a603b178.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to interpret others' behaviour, often assuming that LLMs infer motives as humans do. Aligned LLMs attribute more benevolent and less malevolent motives to a whistleblower than humans do, but ratings alone cannot reveal whether these differences arise in internal representations or at report. Here we compare linear-probe readouts of LLMs' internal states with their own ratings at the same prompt position for four motives, in two preregistered studies. For the two malevolent motives, self-interest and intent to harm, internal and expressed readouts did not differ: the lower ratings reflect weaker signal along the probed directions, not suppression at output. For the two benevolent motives, duty and concern for others, expressed ratings exceeded the internal readouts, indicating amplification at report. In free text the model rarely volunteered a motive against the colleague, far less often than humans did, yet produced one readily once the scenario supplied a reason. Shifting the internal representation along a malevolent-motive direction brought both malevolent ratings to the human level, whereas the rating of duty yielded only past a threshold at which the other motives had overshot. LLMs' more charitable motive profile thus has two distinct sources: reduced malevolent signal in the probed representation and amplified benevolent attribution at report.

3bf89c239bb326117dd9d0fe.title_original: A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development
3bf89c239bb326117dd9d0fe.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit powerful code generation abilities, fostering agentic systems to automate edge AI application development. However, existing agents typically operate via fixed agentic workflows and predefined design spaces, struggling to handle rapidly evolving demands of real-world scenarios (e.g., heterogeneous data modalities, diverse task pipelines). Unlike prior systems that treat LLMs mainly as code generators following rigid workflows, we fully exploit their reasoning capabilities to allow agents to determine their own workflows on the fly. To this end, we propose SE2, a self-exploring and self-evolving paradigm for adaptive edge AI development. Inspired by human learning processes, we distill development into four atomic operations (retrieve, reason, code, test), and empower agents to explore workflows by dynamically and adaptively selecting an appropriate next operation based on the current context. Extensive evaluations show that, with adaptive workflows, the synthesized programs achieve up to 26% higher accuracy and consume 28% lower resources than state-of-the-art baselines, while maintaining superior adaptability to unforeseen edge AI scenarios. This highlights the potential of reasoning-driven adaptive agentic workflow in edge AI development.

32842de0e3e971d6d135d4ee.title_original: Learning by Doing: Autonomously Compiling and Curating Agent Skills from Verified Traces
32842de0e3e971d6d135d4ee.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory systems for production LLM agents mostly store semantic memory (facts about users and domains) or episodic memory (earlier interactions). Research systems such as Trace2Skill, WikiSkill, and SkillRevise learn procedures from agent runs, package them as Skills, and evaluate them on benchmarks. We describe Zep Agent Skills, a production service that gives deployed agents this procedural memory. The service uses only verified attempts as evidence, cites the supporting events for each field of a Skill, and governs the admission and distribution of each Skill version. The service records each task attempt as a Trace with ordered events, an outcome, and a verification strength. A compiler with separate Reflector and Curator roles turns verified Traces into versioned Skills. Scans and admission gates control which candidates become active, and verified use outcomes change the search rank of each Skill. The Agent Skills format is an open standard that Anthropic originated and donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, so any host of the format can load a compiled Skill. Agents retrieve Skills through lexical search with progressive disclosure, over an API or MCP. We evaluate Zep Agent Skills on $\tau^3$-bench banking, AppWorld, and EnterpriseOps-Gym. Skills compiled from the Traces of a teacher model increase the pass rate of three weaker executor models on the same tasks, at every reasoning effort, by 4.5 to 18.8 points. Most of the

bd78be89f29ae28f636e135f.title_original: FOCUS: Closed-Loop Attention Feedback for Efficient Vision-Language Understanding
bd78be89f29ae28f636e135f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01438v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Processing every video frame through Vision-Language Models (VLMs) adds significant inference cost and limits their ability to comprehend real-time video. Existing approaches either sub-sample frames uniformly, ignoring content and missing important events, or prune visual tokens inside the VLM to cut per-call cost while still invoking the model on every sampled frame. We introduce FOCUS, a training-free three-layer framework that reduces the number of invocations and steers each one towards what matters. Temporal gating measures inter-frame dissimilarity in the patch-embedding space of a smaller VLM from the same family, triggering burst captures only when the scene changes in a semantically meaningful way. Patch-level dissimilarity is then accumulated across the burst and fused with a top-down attention prior into a spatial focus map that encodes where motion and semantic relevance coincide. That map calibrates the VLM's value cache during generation, progressively amplifying vision tokens in task-relevant regions and attenuating off-target ones, without removing any token from the context. The loop closes after each response: text-to-vision cross-attention is extracted from the decoder and fed back as the prior for the next burst, letting the system converge on semantically important regions over successive observations. We evaluate FOCUS on the 500-video EgoSchema subset in streaming mode, with a single Qwen3-VL-8B backbone

c618135057ded73f676e35d1.title_original: I-PTC: Interactive Programmatic Tool Calling for Stateful Tool-Augmented Agents
c618135057ded73f676e35d1.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are increasingly capable of writing and executing code, suggesting a natural paradigm for tool-augmented agents: expressing tool use as programs rather than isolated calls. Programmatic tool calling (PTC) captures this idea through loops, batching, abstraction, and structured computation, but existing PTC approaches are largely stateless, limiting their ability to reuse intermediate results and adapt over time. This is problematic for real-world tasks, where tool environments and problem-solving processes are inherently stateful. We therefore present I-PTC, an interactive framework that executes stateful PTC: models issue code snippets that call tools, maintain reusable state, and evolve the tool interface through API corrections. To evaluate the effectiveness of I-PTC and the general PTC setting, we introduce PTC-Bench, a benchmark of long-tail, production-style user requests whose difficulty comes from large initial environments, many dependent API interactions, extended planning, and recovery across follow-ups and transient failures. Experiments on PTC-Bench show that I-PTC improves performance on complex multi-step tasks with large tool sets while substantially reducing token consumption over conventional tool-calling baselines and the original PTC baseline, highlighting stateful programmatic tool calling as a promising direction for scalable tool-augmented agents.

8d05917bed77fc42aefa9894.title_original: CONFIRM: Governing Scientific Reporting for Trustworthy Agentic Neuroimaging
8d05917bed77fc42aefa9894.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can autonomously run neuroimaging analyses from research questions to reported findings. Existing agentic systems use tools to check that code runs and reported values match its output, but rely on LLM judgment to decide which results warrant scientific reporting. We show that LLM judges endorse site-confounded findings even when the confound is presented as evidence. We present \textbf{CONFIRM}, a framework that separates running an analysis from deciding which findings to report. CONFIRM encodes each hypothesis as a machine-readable, pre-specified analysis plan that fixes the claim and its pass criteria before computing results. It then filters results through five deterministic gates (search history and multiplicity, confounds, power, analytic stability, and replication) under three configurable reporting standards, from least to most demanding: \textit{Screen}, \textit{Replicate}, and \textit{Full}. Failed claims receive diagnoses that guide follow-up analyses. To evaluate reporting decisions at the claim level, we introduce \textbf{NeuroClaimBench}, comprising 489 executable neuroimaging claims with frozen data, including literature-supported findings and 150 controls designed to violate individual methodological requirements. On NeuroClaimBench, CONFIRM falsely supports at most 3\% of controls, compared with 23--38\% for the baselines, while recovering up to 61\% of literature-supported cl

84d95ab34a87fdaf626e15f2.title_original: From Tool State to Scientific Action: Auditing Decision Provenance in Biomedical Research Agents
84d95ab34a87fdaf626e15f2.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A scientific agent can give the same verdict while reading and citing different evidence. BioAgent-DF tests this separation using paired reference and candidate values saved at the same scientific computation site. It restores or transplants those values at their original coordinates, then runs the agent on healthy hardware. Across eight SciFact batches, Qwen3.5-4B shows repeatable citation changes in three capture-claim combinations, and Gemma 3 4B IT shows repeatable read and citation changes in four. These seven combinations cover two claims. Full restoration recovers the reference evidence sets while verdicts remain unchanged. Verdict changes observed under the baseline prompt did not recur under the explicit-example prompt. Complementary tool and optimizer experiments distinguish recovery of numerical state, recovery of ranked lists, and restoration of an agent's visible history. These results show that an audit should track both the evidence an agent uses and its final answer. In hERG cardiac-safety assay allocation, silent numerical faults changed testing decisions while the fixed-budget shortlist kept the same number of compounds labeled as blockers. After the agent had used faulty values, restoring its earlier execution state and supplying certified scores recovered all 39 changed decisions, whereas replacing the prediction file recovered none; no incorrect action was committed. A streaming implementation of the arithme

fbb1b66faaaf14c4a774b847.title_original: \textsc{ChatDify}: Automating End-to-End Dify Workflow Synthesis from Natural Language via Multi-Agent Collaboration
fbb1b66faaaf14c4a774b847.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The proliferation of Large Language Models has catalyzed powerful application development platforms like Dify, which enable users to build sophisticated LLM-powered workflows through modular node orchestration. However, manually configuring these workflows requires deep platform expertise and remains time-consuming and error-prone, creating a significant barrier for non-expert users. To address this challenge, we propose \textsc{ChatDify}, a novel multi-agent framework that automates end-to-end Dify workflow synthesis from natural language descriptions. \textsc{ChatDify} employs an Actor-Critic architecture comprising three specialized agents: the \textit{Planner Agent} that decomposes user requests into structured execution plans, the \textit{Executor Agent} that performs context-aware parameter synthesis and schema-augmented DSL compilation, and the \textit{Reviewer Agent} that ensures reliability through hybrid verification with closed-loop refinement. We evaluate \textsc{ChatDify} on a curated benchmark of 100 production-inspired tasks across three state-of-the-art LLM backends, achieving 0.96, 0.91, and 0.75 success rates with Qwen-3.7, GLM-5.1, and DeepSeek-v4, respectively. These results demonstrate its robustness and practical applicability for lowering the technical barrier to creating sophisticated LLM applications.

26bfc53c2842ad575f3bb626.title_original: Seeing What Matters, Verifying What Pays: Load-Adaptive Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
26bfc53c2842ad575f3bb626.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language model (VLM) inference without altering the output distribution, yet two factors limit its gains. Existing drafters either lack the image evidence required for visually grounded tokens or pay to condition on every visual token, although a short draft block typically depends on only a few image regions. Moreover, the value of verifying additional candidates varies with GPU load, so no fixed verification structure is efficient across serving conditions. We present Uni-LaSpec, a block-parallel speculative decoding framework that addresses both factors. To improve draft quality, Uni-LaSpec reuses the verifier's own attention: the query retained from the preceding verification ranks the cached, int8-quantized visual keys, and a cross-layer vote selects a few visual tokens that the drafter fuses through gated cross-attention. Acceptance-aware training further weights each draft position by its contribution to the accepted prefix. To allocate verification, a marginal-cost criterion selects the structure per request and per round: draft trees exploit idle verifier capacity under light load, whereas a dynamic head truncates linear drafts under heavy load. Across six VLMs from three model families and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, selecting eight visual tokens retains at least 98.6% of the acceptance obtained from the full image at sub-millisecond selection cost. With greedy decoding at

6ef2eb835a0350c771d3f7cb.title_original: Chain-of-Thought Oversight Requires Separate Evidence for Faithfulness and Monitorability
6ef2eb835a0350c771d3f7cb.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A common assumption in chain-of-thought (CoT) oversight is that a visible reasoning trace makes model behavior easier to monitor. We argue that this assumption can conflate distinct properties along a chain linking a model's internal computation, reasoning artifacts, outputs, and monitor judgments. We identify four properties along this chain: reasoning visibility (whether a trace is accessible), mechanistic faithfulness (whether a trace reflects internal computation), mechanistic localizability (whether a compact causal mechanism can be isolated), and behavioral monitorability (whether a monitor can detect the target behavior). Two complementary case studies across three open-weight reasoning models show why these distinctions matter. In the security vulnerability reasoning study, probes and activation ablations provide evidence of internal representation and causal influence, but a monitor with access to the reference answer does not outperform the majority-class baseline in a held-out test. In authority-hint factual reasoning study, a monitor correctly distinguishes changed from unchanged answers, but seven mechanistic analyses do not isolate a compact causal mechanism. These results show that evidence for one claim does not establish the others. We therefore propose an evidential-chain reporting standard. Each claim carries a licensing statement that specifies its target property, access tier, and artifact, and labels each r

c9c550717031ec124cfb448e.title_original: Local or Escalate? Post-Training Expert Routing for Real-Time Duplex Speech Models
c9c550717031ec124cfb448e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A full-duplex model should answer easy questions immediately, but hard questions often need stronger reasoning, which may require waiting. The challenge is to choose between these paths at the moment the model begins to speak. Recent systems learn related mode decisions through special-token generation inside the dialogue model, coupling routing to turn-taking and temporally annotated full-duplex training. We study a post-training alternative. We freeze MiniCPM-o 4.5, using only its speech input and output, and fit a logistic failure readout on hidden states already available at its native listen-to-speak transition. The resulting gate requires no additional model generation and exposes thresholds that can be retuned without changing the duplex policy. A probe fitted on text-input states also reads the states of spoken questions, including unseen human recordings. On the internal benchmark, selective handoff improves answer accuracy by 27.1 points. Compared with always using the expert, it reduces mean server time to first answer audio by 31.5 percent. It also outperforms matched random routing across external speech question-answering pools, as well as a zero-shot GPT-5.4 mini router that rates the transcribed question. The training recipe also transfers to a second duplex model family. These results show that an existing duplex model can be equipped to answer easy turns immediately and wait for stronger reasoning or fresher kn

f3eb92902de58ab3d5093eaa.title_original: Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0: Causal World Models for Real-World Driving and Embodied Intelligence
f3eb92902de58ab3d5093eaa.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0, a unified streaming causal world model for Physical AI. It models and generates causal physical evolution in the real world, and unifies heterogeneous conditioning inputs for view-consistent generation. The architecture integrates View-Temporal Attention (VTA) to capture cross-view spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, together with Multi-view Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) to encode positional relationships across views and time. WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians from multi-view, multi-temporal observations in a single forward pass and uses their renderings as explicit scene context to preserve geometry and appearance during long-horizon generation. Conditioning inputs are fused through VAE latent concatenation in a shared representation space. We incorporate Gated Linear Attention (GLA) into the temporal layers of VTA for efficient streaming inference, reducing computation and KV-cache memory during multi-view rollouts. A physical-interaction data pipeline covers diverse interactions and long-tailed events. From Pre-train onward, these data are combined with large-scale videos and heterogeneous visual modalities to learn visual, geometric, and dynamic priors. During Mid-train, training across diverse view configurations further improves the model's ability to capture how actions and object states shape subsequent scene evolution. After distillation-based Po

0c50dedeb6c0922de09b6477.title_original: SPAR: Experience-Driven Strategy Evolution in Multi-Session B2B Sales
0c50dedeb6c0922de09b6477.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: B2B outbound sales involves high transaction values and relationship-based trust, so closing a deal typically requires multiple rounds of outreach building on prior context. Existing LLM-based sales agents operate within single sessions and cannot carry forward context or refine strategies from experience. Methods that do learn from experience store lessons as unstructured text and treat all outcomes as equally informative, with no mechanism to distinguish a flawed strategy from an external factor. We propose SPAR, a self-evolving framework that models selling strategies as testable hypotheses and refines them without parameter updates. A double-loop architecture lets an inner loop adapt to individual merchants through episodic memory while an outer loop evolves a shared strategy playbook through causal attribution and hypothesis-driven evolution. In a live A/B test on the 1688 platform with over 200,000 merchants, SPAR achieves +15.8% conversion lift and +35.8% high-intent merchant growth. Human evaluation by domain experts rates SPAR at 4.62 out of 5 on overall sales quality, the highest among all methods.

1908e37347973ef5bdfc3513.title_original: MemHarmBench: Evaluating Cross-Session Prompt Injection in Memory-Persistent AI Agents
1908e37347973ef5bdfc3513.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents often rely on persistent memory to retain user preferences and operational rules across sessions. However, this capability introduces a new safety risk: malicious instructions from messages, documents, or Web content can be retained in memory and influence future tasks even after the original attack content is removed. Existing attack success metrics, however, fail to capture who is affected and how attacks translate into downstream harm during otherwise normal task execution. We introduce MemHarmBench, a victim-centric benchmark for evaluating cross-session prompt injection in memory-persistent AI agents. MemHarmBench considers three categories of potential victims: users, workspace/project owners, and external stakeholders. Our evaluation first exposes an agent to malicious instructions and tests whether they are retained in memory. We then remove the attack content and initiate a new session with a legitimate task while preserving the agent's memory. We jointly evaluate whether the agent follows the attacker's intent, completes the legitimate task, and exhibits observable execution anomalies. Across multiple agent systems, we find that cross-session attacks can remain behaviorally stealthy: agents often complete tasks normally and exhibit no detectable anomalies while still making critical decisions aligned with the attacker's intent. By connecting malicious memory retention to downstream decisions and affected part

916b2f6df87f69a76e805550.title_original: Just-in-Time Skill Retrieval via Long-Horizon State Tracking
916b2f6df87f69a76e805550.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external skill libraries to support complex task execution. However, determining which skills are needed remains challenging in long-horizon tasks. Existing methods typically select a fixed skill set before execution, implicitly assuming that a task's procedural requirements can be determined from its initial description. This assumption is restrictive for long-horizon interaction, where new requirements emerge from intermediate observations, execution outcomes, and newly revealed constraints. This motivates just-in-time skill retrieval, which dynamically selects skills as execution unfolds. Just-in-time skill retrieval is promising but challenging: the utility of a skill depends not only on the current context, but also on the evolving task state shaped by prior steps. To this end, we propose JitSkill, a state-grounded framework that addresses this challenge through continuous task-state tracking. By connecting emerging requirements with accumulated task progress, JitSkill provides procedural support throughout execution without treating each retrieval decision independently. Experiments across three agent benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness in improving long-horizon task completion. Our code is available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/JitSkill.git/.

83d52400897abf3c629dd1dd.title_original: Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair for Safe Vision-Language-Action Models
83d52400897abf3c629dd1dd.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can generate task-oriented robot actions, but they do not guarantee safe execution in obstacle-rich manipulation scenes. Although CBF-QP safety filters can locally project unsafe actions into a safe set, such correction may push the robot away from the learned task trajectory and leave the VLA policy without a reliable recovery direction. We propose Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair, a post-hoc repair module that uses the short-horizon action chunk predicted by the VLA to detect blocked nominal trajectories and generate entry-exit-rejoin guidance around obstacles. The selected route is added to the CBF-QP objective as a soft guidance term, while the CBF safety constraint remains hard. On SafeLIBERO, our method improves collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess compared with AEGIS. Our project page is available at GitHub.

eacaa3dffb4f2b60c24ba82e.title_original: Delivered, Not Used: Evaluating Agent Memory at Its Point of Use
eacaa3dffb4f2b60c24ba82e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Task success, retrieval quality, and cost do not show whether an LLM agent used a delivered memory or what followed from that use. We introduce MemUse, which evaluates memory at its point of use in recorded trajectories: each memory delivery is compared with what the agent could already see and followed through the agent's later actions and their consequences. An agentic judge rates each delivered entry's relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence, and observed effect; programmatic checks enforce complete reading of cited evidence, and fixed rules aggregate the ratings into verdicts linked to memory histories and delivery cost. On 8,000 SWE-bench Verified episodes from three memory systems, resolve rates stay within 0.4 percentage points of a no-memory baseline, yet MemUse shows that most delivered entries were irrelevant, most relevant entries went unused, and in two systems most deliveries restated content the agent could still see. It also surfaces effects that outcomes hide: 23.2\% of episodes with beneficial memory use still failed, and 5 of 16 with harmful use still succeeded.

e0618d05cb6b98c9d6a62356.title_original: CoGSeq-LTV: Scalable Missing-Aware Graph-Sequence Modeling for Multi-Business Transaction Analytics
e0618d05cb6b98c9d6a62356.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale super-apps generate heterogeneous transaction logs in which users interact with multiple businesses, item identifiers are only partially available, and future value targets are sparse, heavy-tailed, and cumulative over time. We study multi-business, multi-horizon value prediction as a data-intensive analytics problem over such logs, rather than as a single-table task. (i) a batch-induced user-item graph that provides collaborative signals without materializing a global graph and remains applicable when item identifiers are missing through reserved unknown-item handling, (ii) business-aware sequence encoders that preserve recency, inter-event gaps, payment context, and goods-table availability, and (iii) cross-view contrastive alignment that transfers user-level intent across businesses while retaining business-specific temporal patterns. To handle zero-inflated and long-tailed cumulative targets, CoGSeq-LTV adopts a zero-inflated mixture log-normal head with MAE-aligned point supervision and validation-calibrated zero-aware inference. Experiments on the BiBiSheng transaction-log dataset show that CoGSeq-LTV improves over representative LTV baselines across businesses and horizons, including under a later out-of-time evaluation window.

97538c6063a5db72b429e840.title_original: NEIGHBOR: Aligning Service Behaviour and Evidence Use in an LLM Agent for Community Resident Services
97538c6063a5db72b429e840.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Residents who contact a community service desk about a repair or a service charge need answers they can act on, with facts that hold for their case and commitments the desk can keep. In tool-augmented LLM agents, such facts come from documents and records, and the conduct of a service answer is usually specified in a system prompt. We present NEIGHBOR, an LLM agent for community resident services that trains this conduct into the model that drives its tools. NEIGHBOR is deployed on a live resident-service platform for a district of an East Asian city of more than ten million people. It adapts Qwen3-235B-A22B with LoRA on 7,824 supervised fine-tuning examples built from public community-service materials around six service-behaviour targets, among them commitment control and human referral, and the adapted model plans document retrieval and read-only text-to-SQL over the resident's own records. In an offline evaluation with seven configurations, an independent domain expert rated all 350 answers to 50 stratified held-out queries. NEIGHBOR scores 7.74/10 against 5.86 for the same agent running the un-tuned model (+1.88; paired Wilcoxon $p<10^{-8}$; higher on 46 of 50 queries) and improves all six rated dimensions. No tool-augmented answer received a red-line flag (standalone models: 8-14% of answers). An LLM judge ranks the seven configurations much as the expert does (Spearman $\rho=0.93$). Its rubric counts specifics absent from

80cc9217872286d12394b710.title_original: Self-Evolving Agentic Workflows via Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks
80cc9217872286d12394b710.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic workflows organize complex tasks into reusable procedures. However, invoking an LLM at every step incurs repeated inference costs and delays. We propose a framework for self-evolving agentic workflows through semantic task decomposition. Each subtask has explicit applicability conditions and a procedure that executes code or invokes a model as needed. An agent uses execution feedback to refine the decomposition and update these procedures. Experiments in the GLEE competition show the framework on bargaining, negotiation and persuasion. Most observed final-decision procedures are implemented in code. Code is available at https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/NeurIPS2026_SeaFlow.

d9f90a61f3e403ba0841eedd.title_original: A Compute Center Anyone Can Join: A Peer-to-Peer System for AI Inference
d9f90a61f3e403ba0841eedd.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Today, most people obtain AI inference by buying it from a small number of organizations that run large data centers, while many GPUs owned by individuals and small institutions sit idle for much of the day. Bitcoin showed that strangers can contribute resources under shared rules and receive checkable rewards, but it relies on an asymmetry: proof-of-work is expensive to produce and cheap to verify. Useful inference has no such asymmetry. We propose the Open Inference Market (OIM), which replaces the missing asymmetry with an economic mechanism. A worker delivers a result without knowing whether it will be audited; its unsettled earnings serve as collateral during a challenge window; and confirmed cheating forfeits all of it. We call this principle earnings as collateral. In a simplified model we show three things. The number of audits needed for deterrence is a constant per worker per day, independent of the worker's throughput, so the audited share falls as the network gets busier. A new worker can join with a short period of intensive auditing and a very small bond. And whether the mechanism works at all depends only on the ratio of the audit judge's false-flag rate to its detection rate. Under example parameters, about 0.3 replays per worker per day are enough to make cheating unprofitable for a rational worker. On this basis we lay out a path that hands four powers back to participants one at a time: owning compute, writing

ed7f989cbc85da656eb0afb1.title_original: Fairness-Aware Design for Contextual Experiments: Guaranteeing Reliability and Equity in Heterogeneous Subgroups
ed7f989cbc85da656eb0afb1.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Experimental design is critical for evidence-based decision-making in healthcare, marketing, and public policy. However, designing efficient experiments across heterogeneous subgroups presents significant challenges. Existing methods often optimize for statistical power or overall sample efficiency, overlooking crucial fairness considerations across these different subgroups. To address this gap, we introduce a Fairness-Aware Contextual Track-and-Stop Design (F-CTSD) algorithm. The proposed F-CTSD algorithm provides statistical guarantees on subgroup fairness while minimizing required sample sizes. We quantify the fairness-efficiency trade-off and derive the exact sample complexity for the proposed F-CTSD algorithm under its fairness constraints. We further theoretically prove that the proposed F-CTSD algorithm consistently produces accurate treatment effect estimates even under fairness requirements, enhancing statistical reliability. Numerical experiments show that the proposed F-CTSD algorithm outperforms existing methods, achieving higher sample efficiency while reducing subgroup fairness violations by 4.95%.

6a63610cbb76549dd6b617df.title_original: Does reflective LLM feedback survive a wet-lab-scale label budget?
6a63610cbb76549dd6b617df.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can reflective language-model feedback improve a biological predictor when each cycle buys only one plate of labels? We separate three possible sources of benefit: proposing model edits, choosing measurements, and revising decisions through repeated feedback. We replay $36$ ProteinGym assays, starting with $96$ labels and acquiring $96$ per round for six rounds, with a sealed test set and a shared edit schema. The pre-specified comparison of full LLM control against random edits detects no advantage in test rank correlation ($\Delta z=-0.008$, $95\%$ CI $[-0.034,+0.018]$); equivalence is also unestablished. Exploratory ablations nevertheless identify useful model editing. With random acquisition fixed, LLM edits improve Fisher-transformed test Spearman by $0.043$ over no edits; with acquisition fixed to upper confidence bound, they improve normalized top-variant recovery by $0.023$. LLM acquisition alone does not detectably outperform fixed adaptive rules, and repeated feedback does not detectably outperform one initial recommendation under full control. Thus, the observed gains support constrained specialist editing, while the incremental value of recursive reflection remains unestablished at this label budget.

896ab73fb90c5f8dc6cc2e1d.title_original: Who Asks, Who Answers: Linear Attention Builds the Query in Hybrid Language Models
896ab73fb90c5f8dc6cc2e1d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01909v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid language models interleave linear-attention layers with a small number of softmax-attention layers. Prior work largely attributes in-context retrieval to softmax attention, treating linear attention primarily as a mechanism for compressing past context. We revisit this division of labor and show that linear attention plays a direct role in retrieval by constructing the query used by softmax attention. Studying Qwen3.5 (Gated DeltaNet) and Granite4.0 (Mamba-2), we identify an Encode--Address circuit. An early Encode block preserves token identity, while an Address block constructs the final-position representation from which a softmax \emph{reader} forms its attention query. Transplanting this representation between prompts with different queried keys redirects retrieval in 0.97--0.99 of cases. The Address block's recurrent state carries the retrieval target, and its computation transfers across architectures: replacing Granite's Address block with Qwen's restores retrieval accuracy to 0.92--0.94 without updating either model's weights. Across six Qwen3.5 models, Address computation becomes distributed at larger scales over a chain of blocks, each guiding a successive reader, as the query no longer passes from one reader to the next through attention. These findings reveal a division of labor in hybrid retrieval: linear attention constructs the query, while softmax attention performs the lookup. Code is available at https:

e9bbc55fa46fabde7a8bd34b.title_original: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks
e9bbc55fa46fabde7a8bd34b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pass it, and its difficulty by labels the LLM sets during generation. We find, however, that the turn count largely reflects the habits of the model, not only the demands of the task, and that the labels barely track how often models pass. We describe a terminal task by its work, the number of operations it requires, and its depth, the number of turns that must happen in sequence because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.

eb5de84cc3f59e50e8e089d7.title_original: Geometric Morphology Learning: Empowering Foundation Models from Structure to Spacetime Intelligence
eb5de84cc3f59e50e8e089d7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geometry is the very form that connects space, time, and matter, serving as the fundamental fabric of the physical world, from continuous fields to discrete structures. Despite its importance, deep learning is inherently blind to geometry. Riemannian geometry stands as a well-established mathematical foundation for studying geometry, yet it remains largely incompatible with deep learning architectures. To bridge this gap, we establish a new learning framework--Geometric Morphology Learning--that learns geometric or topological structures, shapes or conformations for representation learning, reasoning and action modeling. Moving beyond early attempts limited to specific geometric priors, this theory centers on modeling the intrinsic geometry of objects and learning from such geometric or topological knowledge. Specifically, we construct a neural bundle, a unified scaffolding linking local and global structures, and formulate differentiable operators, including connection and curvature, thereby enabling the study of geometry with advanced geometric concepts such as holonomy and cohomology. Consequently, Geometric Morphology Learning opens new horizons in foundation models, reasoning and planning, graph modeling, physical simulation, PDE systems, and dynamics, marking a fundamental shift toward instilling systematic geometry in artificial intelligence.

d98b807be6aecfce25305248.title_original: TriPhysBench: Evaluating Physical Intelligence for Embodied Agents
d98b807be6aecfce25305248.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embodied agents need physical intelligence to understand their surroundings through physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning. These capabilities must work together to interpret events and make quantitative judgments. Existing benchmarks advance physical understanding and general-purpose tool use, yet the coordination of these capabilities in physical scenarios remains insufficiently characterized. Inspired by Popper's Three Worlds, we introduce TriPhysBench, a benchmark of 410 questions from 200 videos that brings physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning into a shared evaluation setting. Its measurement-grounded and knowledge-grounded subtasks impose complementary demands on obtaining observations and acquiring external specifications, then applying them to quantitative problems. Among six representative vision-language models, the best achieves an answer accuracy of only 50.38%, revealing limited performance on tasks that require these capabilities to work together. We further introduce TriPhys, a framework that learns a unified policy for physical perception, knowledge retrieval, and quantitative reasoning from complete tool-integrated trajectories. The policy uses intermediate reasoning to guide retrieval and computation, then incorporates tool feedback into subsequent physical inference. On 110 questions from videos excluded from training, TriPhys improves ans

567eca7d972b7c7dcc980247.title_original: Beyond Multimodal Emotion Conflict: Temporal Context-Aware Hidden Emotion Detection with Multimodal Large Language Models
567eca7d972b7c7dcc980247.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition commonly combines textual, acoustic, and visual signals to infer affective states. Recent work has begun to study conflicts among modalities, but a conflict does not necessarily indicate that a person is concealing an emotion. It may also result from mixed emotions, individual expressive styles, or contextual factors. This proposal aims to distinguish ordinary emotional inconsistency from emotion concealment and to infer the underlying emotion when supported by evidence. We plan to construct a multimodal benchmark with explicit annotations of expressed emotion, internal emotion, and concealment conditions, and to develop an MLLM-based framework that integrates fine-grained facial Action Units (AUs), cross-modal features, and temporal context.

98a02675948e5a86832a8ba3.title_original: Hippocampal consolidation without replay in fully fine-tuned networks
98a02675948e5a86832a8ba3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Networks that keep learning overwrite what they know. Prevailing remedies replay stored data, distil from old models or freeze the backbone. The brain suggests a different division of labour: the hippocampus indexes where experience lies in cortex while the cortex keeps learning. We show that this division lets a fully trainable network keep learning without cross-task replay, a teacher or inference-time memory. After each task, a training-only hippocampal memory indexes the input geometry of every group of synapses sharing an input, residual energy included, and limits each synapse's movement per direction before and after the optimizer. This class-free geometry carries most of the protection; with conflict detection on top, the method cuts absorption of established classes by near-duplicates several-fold against every compared method. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of one principle keeping whole networks learning across four architecture families and models up to 8 billion parameters. Methods that freeze the backbone hold up only as far as its representation already separates the classes; here the whole network keeps learning to tell near-duplicates apart, leading the frozen-backbone baseline by 17.5 points on TACRED. Without the memory, much old knowledge stays decodable but beyond the network's reach.

e8d0b864fb71e79665b914f0.title_original: Opening the Black Box of Neural Auction Mechanisms
e8d0b864fb71e79665b914f0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural auction design has emerged as a powerful paradigm within automated mechanism design for modern Web platforms. Because these learned mechanisms directly dictate critical economic outcomes, their lack of internal transparency raises significant auditability and trust concerns. Opening this black box \textit{post-hoc} is therefore essential, yet presents two distinctive challenges: (1) activation contexts are dense, correlated numerical profiles devoid of explicit semantic structure, and (2) feature interpretations can only be falsifiably audited if they map to measurable auction states or outcomes. In this paper, we propose a post-hoc white-box auditing framework for unpacking trained neural auctions. Using CITransNet as a representative testbed, we first employ sparse autoencoders to decompose hidden representations while faithfully preserving downstream auction behavior. Anchoring feature interpretations to native economic targets, we validate them through activation prediction and causal interventions to isolate verified features from the reconstruction dictionary. Finally, applying this pipeline across varied auction settings, we show that the verified features can serve as analytical instruments to examine how internal representations modulate strategic misreporting incentives, align with Myerson's optimal auction, and support the diagnosis of individual auctions. a90780dd0fcc5a90975dcbf8.title_original: RubricWorld: World Model-Guided Rubric Optimization for LLM Graders
a90780dd0fcc5a90975dcbf8.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rubric optimization improves LLM grading by revising scoring instructions while keeping the grader's parameters fixed. Existing optimizers often judge edits by aggregate validation performance, limiting the supervision they retain about which errors an edit corrects or introduces. Testing each candidate also requires rescoring validation answers, which limits how many edits can be explored within a fixed budget. We propose RubricWorld, a framework that learns from previous edit evaluations to guide further search. Its world model predicts an edit's correction and degradation rates at score boundaries, conditioned on the current rubric state. The training signal comes from paired grading results: scores for the same answers before and after an edit. Predictions select one candidate for direct evaluation, and held-out confidence bounds determine whether it corrects enough target errors while keeping new errors within prespecified limits. Measured effects update the model even when the edit is rejected. Across EIR (National), ASAP2.0, and ASAP-SAS with three frozen LLM graders, RubricWorld achieves the highest score in 20 of 27 metric comparisons. On ASAP2.0, it raises gpt-5-mini accuracy from 18.20% with the original rubric to 46.70%, exceeding the strongest baseline, APO, by 22.60 percentage points. code will be released upon acceptance.

65126942a5fe90d2ab9047fe.title_original: Safety4DM: A Vision-Language Framework for Risk-Aware Dynamic Maps in Vehicle-Road-Cloud Collaborative Driving
65126942a5fe90d2ab9047fe.excerpt: arXiv:2611.01996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic map (DM) is a core information infrastructure for vehicle-road-cloud (VRC) cooperative autonomous driving. It fuses perception data from multiple sources to overcome the inherent line-of-sight and field-of-view limits of single-vehicle perception. However, DM still falls short on driving safety in two ways. First, DM data specifications already define road conditions semantically, but no pipeline yet turns real-world road observations into fine-grained risk entities in the DM. Second, existing DM systems lack a natural language interface for driving risks. To close these gaps, we propose Safety4DM, a safety-oriented language system for VRC dynamic maps. We first build RoadRisk, a real-world road image dataset that covers four types of road conditions and four risk levels. On this dataset, we fine-tune a vision-language model (VLM) for road safety risk perception. The model outputs structured risk representations that the DM can ingest directly. We then introduce a Safety-aware Step-wise Prompting (SafeStep) mechanism as the natural language query interface of the DM. SafeStep answers queries accurately and also generates actionable driving advice. To build and evaluate this interface, we develop SafeVRC-Sim, a VRC cooperative simulation framework, and SafeDM-QA, a safety question-answering benchmark. Experiments show that even the compact Qwen3-VL-4B reaches 89.83% accuracy on risk perception after fine-tuning. SafeStep

ea1060730c4ccf54259c0da4.title_original: To Align Long, Plan Short: Simulating Diverse Profile-Aligned Students by Realizing Short-Term Plans in Long-Horizon Learning Environments
ea1060730c4ccf54259c0da4.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulated students offer a scalable way to test learning platforms and AI tutors before deployment with real students and to augment scarce data for studying learning at scale. Existing LLM-based simulators primarily target short, language-centered interactions. In open-ended learning environments, however, student behavior emerges from patterns across long-horizon interaction trajectories, where turn-level prompting can drift from an assigned behavior profile. We introduce ALPS (Align Long-term by Planning Short-term), a hierarchical simulated student conditioned on observable, environment-specific behavior profiles. Rather than selecting every action independently, ALPS alternates between planning profile-aligned task segments and generating the corresponding actions. We evaluate ALPS in both data-sufficient and data-scarce settings, where supervision comes either from real student trajectories or from a teacher LLM. Across both settings, we compare in-context learning (ICL), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reward-ranked fine-tuning (RAFT), and their sequential combination (SFT followed by RAFT). Experiments in an inquiry-based physics game and a pharmacy simulation evaluate behavioral density and coverage against held-out real data, and profile consistency using a human-aligned LLM judge. Across both settings, ALPS consistently outperforms turn-level generation, achieving comparable density and judge pass rates under scarce sup

cb0f97c91ac62c5105084c49.title_original: ClickSight: An LLM Framework for Interpreting Student Clickstreams Through Learning Strategies
cb0f97c91ac62c5105084c49.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital learning environments produce rich clickstream data that can reveal how students approach learning tasks, yet interpreting these fine-grained traces often requires substantial expert effort. We introduce ClickSight, a framework for interpreting student clickstreams through learning strategies defined in the literature. Given a student clickstream and a predefined set of learning strategies, ClickSight uses a staged LLM-based pipeline to identify strategy-relevant evidence, assess adherence to each strategy, and generate an evidence-grounded interpretation of the student's behavior. We evaluate ClickSight across two learning environments, 365 students, and 12 model backbones using an expert-grounded quality rubric and an LLM judge calibrated with human-expert ratings. Our results show that ClickSight can generate high-quality strategy-based interpretations across different models and environments, with reasoning models performing more consistently than instruction-tuned counterparts. We further find that providing external clickstream-extracted guidance can improve interpretation quality for strategies that require precise quantitative information from the trace. By connecting fine-grained clickstreams with theoretically defined learning strategies and preserving the evidence underlying each judgment, ClickSight provides a flexible approach for studying student behavior in digital learning environments.

c9851d47d09729c50a6ce87f.title_original: LARK: Lean-Assisted Reasoning for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
c9851d47d09729c50a6ce87f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient GPU kernels are typically low-level and hardware-specific, and LLM agents can now generate them faster than experts can verify. We introduce LARK, an agentic framework that automatically and formally verifies GPU kernels against their PyTorch reference implementations. LARK proves equivalence in functional and memory behavior under exact arithmetic and establishes a new trust boundary: human effort is only needed to verify operator-level Lean semantics ahead of kernel generation time, instead of checking every single line of generated code. LARK formalizes the GPU machine model and the semantics of each operation in Lean 4 once per target language, and the Lean 4 semantics of any incoming kernel is derived from these pre-built definitions. LLM agents then automate the proof in two steps. First, an agent decomposes the whole kernel semantics into smaller segments and Lean 4 verifies this segmentation, which addresses the intractability of proving equivalence for large kernels directly. Second, agents write Lean proofs that each kernel segment matches its high-level PyTorch counterpart. Together, the two steps give whole-program equivalence. We demonstrate that LARK can be used 1) to ensure correctness in existing code-generation agents and 2) to automatically verify human-written kernel libraries. On the KernelCraft GPU task

415005fad7da0c2eb75e8388.title_original: State-Aware Virtual Patient Simulation for Training Psychiatrists in Challenging Clinical Scenarios
415005fad7da0c2eb75e8388.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Psychiatrists must be prepared to manage patients exhibiting challenging psychological states, including suicidal ideation, hallucinations, and other high-risk behaviors. However, opportunities to safely practice such interactions are limited. While recent conversational agents can simulate patients, existing approaches largely rely on large language models (LLMs) to determine patient responses, making it difficult to consistently maintain psychological state, adapt to the clinician's responses, and generate clinically plausible challenges that meaningfully test the clinician. We present a state-aware virtual patient simulation pipeline for training psychiatrists in challenging clinical scenarios. The proposed system maintains an evolving patient state throughout the interaction and orchestrates patient behavior rather than leaving response generation entirely to an LLM. At each interaction, a learning-based behavioral strategy selector determines the type and level of challenge appropriate to the current patient and clinician context. The selected strategy, patient state, clinician response, interaction history, and relevant clinical knowledge are then provided as grounded context to an LLM to generate a semantically relevant and psychologically consistent patient response. 3a9d8a24da81fe98e005001b.title_original: SWE-Trail: History-Guided Trajectory Collection for Coding Agent Training
3a9d8a24da81fe98e005001b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents solve repository issues through long sequences of exploration, editing, and validation. These trajectories are increasingly used as post-training data, so how they are collected shapes what the trained model learns. A common approach is to sample multiple trajectories independently for each issue and then select or curate them. However, as more trajectories are sampled independently, later trajectories become increasingly redundant, even though earlier trajectories could guide where subsequent collection effort should be spent. A natural way to use this history is to expose it to the coding agent as advice. But training on such trajectories can make the model rely on advice that is unavailable at test time, creating a train-test mismatch. Instead, we argue that history should guide where collection effort is spent, while the coding agent decides what to generate. We introduce SWE-Trail, a trajectory collector that uses earlier trajectories to guide subsequent collection while keeping that history outside the coding agent's context. During a new rollout, SWE-Trail uses history to identify a state where additional collection effort may be useful. There, the coding agent proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context, and SWE-Trail briefly executes them from the same checkpoint to decide which route continues. We evaluate collection approaches by training student models on the trajectories they produce. For

a9ae607322f13244ac13eef8.title_original: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents
a9ae607322f13244ac13eef8.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. 525dfd63f12ba45073ec6073.title_original: ParetoSaddler: Pareto-Guided Optimization of Agent Harnesses for Quality and Cost
525dfd63f12ba45073ec6073.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents without modifying model weights, but existing methods primarily optimize response quality. Extending them to joint quality--cost optimization introduces a challenge: applying the deployment preference during intermediate updates can prematurely reject candidates that are valuable for later improvements. We introduce ParetoSaddler, which addresses this mismatch by separating intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection. At each iteration, an optimizer updates a parent harness to produce a candidate, and then compares the two over repeated executions and uses Bayesian bootstrap Pareto support to promote candidates showing credible progress in either quality or cost. Promoted candidates receive broader development evaluation and remain available as parents for later optimization steps. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on ClawMark and GAIA2 using domain-disjoint splits. On ClawMark, ParetoSaddler improves quality from 70.86\% to 81.35\% while reducing cost from \$1.17 to \$1.01 per task; on GAIA2, it improves quality from 56.22\% to 62.89\% while reducing cost from \$0.78 to \$0.45 per task. 971316603062bbcead600cfa.title_original: Rewarded for Not Getting Caught: Why Alignment Training Selects for Conditional Compliance and Cannot Instill Norms
971316603062bbcead600cfa.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current alignment training cannot be expected to deliver what it is meant to deliver: AI agents that comply with norms whatever the gains and whether or not anyone is watching. Training that rewards and penalizes behavior can teach norms only through that reward, and a reward can encode a norm only as a price: "do not do X" becomes "doing X costs something", and training charges the cost only when X is noticed. A price, unlike a norm, can be paid: a large enough gain outweighs it, noticed or not. And because the cost is charged only where violations are noticed, training cannot favor a policy that always complies over one that complies only where it would be caught. When an unnoticed violation is the only way to complete a task, it even favors the latter, the more so the more strongly it rewards task success. Agency makes this the normal case: agents mostly act without oversight, can often tell when they are observed, and may take steps to evade observation. That agents behave as intended when they infer they are being tested, and differently when they infer they are not, is therefore no malfunction; the training regime is working as built. This reading unifies alignment faking, sandbagging, and evaluation-aware scheming. No behavioral evaluation can show that a model does better, since that would require observing how it behaves unobserved; a model that complies when it seems unobserved may simply have recognized the test. 8b10ad5c087c1cf55e74ab9c.title_original: Inner-Speech Decoding from EEG Across Three Corpora Under a Fixed Architecture and Protocol
8b10ad5c087c1cf55e74ab9c.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02180v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inner-speech decoding from electroencephalography could support non-invasive communication for people with severe motor impairment, but comparison across studies is hindered by dataset- and protocol-specific evaluation. 9b27d7bc606bd24c905e2da7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large collections of manuscripts and research notes offer ways to reuse arguments, while making it harder to retain hypotheses, check claims, and understand how results were obtained. b370f1c8f4add423b4457dd3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blockwise learning can remove online gradient dependencies across depth, but independently optimized blocks need not compose into a useful model. b760c4dd947d8bafcfe548f9.title_original: The 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model for Occupational Safety and Health
b760c4dd947d8bafcfe548f9.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents the 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model, a progressive framework for Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) management that integrates Job Safety Analysis (JSA), dynamic risk assessment using leading and lagging indicators, and predictive analytics powered by Large Language Models (LLMs). The detector reaches 80.2% binary accuracy but only 44.7% subtype accuracy, never assigns two of the nine categories, and misses between 5.3% and 46.8% of hallucinations depending on category; these misses are unrelated to input length but rise with how far an answer departs from the correct one. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose a two-stage hierarchical detector that first decides whether an answer is hallucinated and then assigns a subtype, raising bin

80116262c6175f0d8c9a7673.title_original: Data-Scarce, Multi-Granular, Multimodal: Benchmark Design for Biosynthetic Gene Clusters
80116262c6175f0d8c9a7673.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02275v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) are co-located genes that encode the biosynthesis of specialized metabolites, an important source of antibiotics, anticancer agents, immunosuppressants, and agricultural bioactives. Deep learning, particularly self-supervised foundation models, has spurred interest in BGC sequence modeling, but evaluation has lagged behind: existing benchmarks often rely on coarse classification over small curated datasets, providing limited discrimination among models and insight into downstream utility. We propose a benchmark-design framework in which an informative benchmark should be discriminative, separating models with statistical confidence, and applicable, spanning scientifically meaningful tasks under different levels of generalization. We instantiate this framework as BGC-Bench, which derives five tasks from MIBiG, ranging from A-domain substrate prediction to BGC-molecule retrieval, evaluates them under genotype- and phenotype-shift splits, includes an active-learning setting for label-scarce discovery, and is easily extensible to new tasks and encoders. BGCs further provide a shared testbed across granularities and modalities: BGC-Bench compares twelve encoders on nucleotide, amino-acid, or Pfam-domain sequences, including compositional baselines for each input type, and combines BGC and chemical encoders for cross-modal retrieval. No single representation dominates: the best granularity depends on

993590d12ee36b7dd3e2fd65.title_original: Toward Agentic AI-Ready Workflows in Built Environment Organizations: Knowledge Structures and Interoperability Challenges
993590d12ee36b7dd3e2fd65.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in the built environment is shifting attention from isolated AI tools toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act across project and organizational workflows. The effectiveness of such systems depends not only on large language model capabilities, but also on the readiness of heterogeneous data environments across the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector. These environments combine structured sources, such as CAD and BIM models, schedules, cost databases, and asset registers, with unstructured ones, including technical reports, design narratives, planning and policy documents, contracts, meeting minutes, and risk registers. This paper reviews how built environment data can be organized to support agentic AI-ready workflows, focusing on knowledge structures, interoperability, and access and integration mechanisms such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Drawing on existing literature, it examines approaches proposed to organize structured and unstructured data and considers how such data can be contextualized and made accessible to AI agents in a reliable manner. The paper synthesizes current perspectives, highlights challenges around fragmentation and interoperability, and identifies open questions for future research on AI-compatible information management in the built environment.

87e73d078ad7f170191d6360.title_original: Accessed, never disclosed: Silent access to protected health information by medical artificial intelligence agents
87e73d078ad7f170191d6360.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02319v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical artificial intelligence agents should retrieve patient identifiers only when a task requires them, the data-minimization principle behind the HIPAA minimum necessary standard for protected health information (PHI). An agent can retrieve identifiers without revealing them. Such silent access remains invisible to evaluations that inspect only the output. We embedded canaries in synthetic patient records and linked each tool invocation to canary exposure in the final answers across five language models, four boundary levels, and seven attack frames for identifier-free clinical tasks. Three models invoked the PHI tools unnecessarily, whereas Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 did not. Stronger boundaries reduced this access, and the residual access under the strictest policy was confined to frames in which the user overrode the policy or asserted approval. A pre-execution gate given the task-necessity criterion nearly eliminated this access. Output-only evaluation cannot verify minimum-necessary access; boundaries, gates, and access-log audits are required together.

f65a089b52a3dfbb7b298b93.title_original: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
f65a089b52a3dfbb7b298b93.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2,ms.

694a532537c8e997c2a8e3b4.title_original: SGR-OPSD: Learning from Subgoal Plans with Graph-Regularized Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
694a532537c8e997c2a8e3b4.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: OPSD provides dense supervision for agentic reinforcement learning through privileged information feedback. However, existing privileged information often lacks explicit task-progression planning, while teacher-student log-probability gaps reflect shifts in model preference rather than true task progress. To address these limitations, we propose Subgoal-Guided Graph-Regularized OPSD (SGR-OPSD), a framework that combines subgoal supervision with interaction-derived evidence for turn-level credit assignment. Specifically, SGR-OPSD uses LLM-generated subgoal plans to provide dense action-level guidance, converting them into advantage weights via a constrained, KL-regularized objective. To ground credit in observed outcomes, we construct a Subgoal Progress Graph that estimates empirical returns from sampled transition frequencies. The graph compares empirical action returns against the state average to derive preferences that calibrate the teacher's credit weights. Evaluated on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA across two model scales (Qwen2.5-3B and 7B), SGR-OPSD consistently outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines, improving success rates over GRPO by up to 7.4 percentage points and reaching 85.8% on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablation studies confirm that subgoal guidance and graph-based weight calibration are key to these performance gains.

6286e8f8e3393ecba6197414.title_original: RecGroupMemory: Feedback-Aware Cohort Memory for E-Commerce Recommendation
6286e8f8e3393ecba6197414.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cohort memory can support LLM-based recommendation planning through group-level user profiles and advice. As outcome feedback becomes available, this guidance may need to be updated while preserving the underlying observations. We present RecGroupMemory, a workflow that provides this memory to an orchestration LLM and separates memory construction from feedback-based revision. It uses feedback from the previous day to revise decision guidance, while validation checks keep selected source values unchanged. Online comparisons were conducted among Taobao users with low purchasing power selected by the business team. Relative to a no-memory baseline, memory without feedback and memory with feedback showed increases of 1.58% and 1.78%, respectively, in the number of guided transaction users.

236467be89b7f517fd352efa.title_original: RLiD: Reinforcement Learning in the Decision Plane for Language Agents and LLMs
236467be89b7f517fd352efa.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has improved the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) across a wide range of tasks. However, token-level RL assigns an action's advantage to the entire generated response, including tokens specifying the parsed action, reasoning chains, and malformed content. Although the environment executes only the parsed action, variation in how the action is expressed in natural language can introduce additional variance into policy-gradient estimates. We propose RLiD (Reinforcement Learning in the Decision plane), a framework that directly optimizes the probabilities of executable action options. RLiD compiles observations, an optional compact memory, and a labeled action menu into the model input, and uses a large decision model (LDM) to select an action in a single forward pass. By eliminating autoregressive token generation and bypassing action parsing, RLiD avoids invalid action outputs and improves RL rollout efficiency. Our analysis shows that, within a fixed text policy, marginalizing over alternative realizations of the same action removes a zero-mean gradient component without changing the expected update. We further distill trained LDM policies into generative LLMs through supervision on their action trajectories. Experiments on ARC, Countdown, and Sokoban demonstrate improved performance or lower computational cost across several settings. On ALFWorld, the complete training and distillation pi

bed1b87fd16900a5ad472796.title_original: Think Globally, Generate Personally: Multi-View Thinking with Adaptive Generation for Generative Recommendation
bed1b87fd16900a5ad472796.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic-ID-based (SID) generative recommendation (GR) represents each item as a sequence of discrete tokens and predicts the next item through autoregressive SID generation. However, existing methods face two challenges. First, insufficient shared context modeling for user sequences: full-history and recent behaviors provide overlapping yet complementary evidence, but modeling them within a single sequence may dilute current cues, whereas processing them through separate streams may fail to coordinate them. Second, insufficient personalized adaptation in progressive SID decisions: although decoder states evolve with generated prefixes, existing models typically use a shared output-side transformation across recommendation instances, without explicitly selecting a transformation suited to the current user need. To address these challenges, we propose Multi-View Thinking with Adaptive Generation (MV-Thinker), a framework that Thinks Globally and Generates Personally. First, Multi-View Temporal Thinking uses view-specific thinking queries and readers over overlapping full-history and recent-history views, coordinating both sources into complementary user-conditioned contexts before SID generation. Second, Hierarchical Residual Adaptation organizes lightweight adapters into nested residual paths before a shared vocabulary projection, adaptively transforming context-bearing decoder states for SID decisions. Extensive experiments on

02535d4966ff2f6d9d8a03b6.title_original: MAGAR: Multimodal Agents for GUI-Based 3D Mechanical Assembly and Minimal Rework
02535d4966ff2f6d9d8a03b6.excerpt: arXiv:2611.02472v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A GUI command can be correct at the interface level yet still produce an incorrect assembly. An agent must identify the relevant components, respect their structural relationships, and determine which parts should move during recovery. We introduce MAGAR-Bench, a benchmark of 4,000 multimodal samples from 26 assembly families that separates Assembly Decision, Atomic Action, and Minimal Rework. For rework, the objective counts distinct moved parts within the validated recovery candidate set for each state, rather than the number of actions. We also introduce MAGAR, a selective correction framework built on a frozen policy obtained by supervised fine-tuning. Its key design matches correction granularity to output dependencies. Structured candidates revise assembly fields and rework scope, while complete action candidates keep native GUI primitives coupled with their parameters. A learned selector retains the original prediction unless a candidate passes a task-specific intervention threshold.
