b44fb05df84d5b7336fff10c.title_original: RecoAtlas: A Benchmark and RL Environment for LLM Recommendation Agents Optimizing Set-Level Utility
b44fb05df84d5b7336fff10c.excerpt: arXiv:2605.18805v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM recommender agents increasingly produce structured reports: sets of items accompanied by natural-language justifications. Yet existing benchmarks often focus on reranking small candidate sets or judging reports primarily by semantic plausibility, providing limited support for evaluating and training agents based on set-level utility. We introduce Recommender Atlas (Agentic Tasks for Learning and Assessment in Shopping), or RecoAtlas, a benchmark and reinforcement learning environment grounded in user behavior. RecoAtlas provides a shopping toolkit for product retrieval, complementarity, and diversity. Given a shopping query, an agent uses these tools to generate a structured recommendation report. Behavioral reference sets support exact-recovery evaluation and the training of a learned bundle-level reward that supplies feedback for policy optimization with RL. Its controlled tool environment exposes agents to semantic and behavior-aligned tools, enabling systematic analysis of how LLM reasoning, tool signals, and tool-use policies contribute to performance. Across controlled experiments, performance scales with model capacity and test-time compute, and improves with stronger tools, while semantic plausibility does not necessarily translate into behavior-grounded utility. RecoAtlas provides a foundation for training and evaluating shopping assistants to move beyond semantic plausibility toward coherent, behaviorally

f36f705960b15f803829a8b7.title_original: Towards Error-Free EHRs: Reasoning-Intensive Consistency Verification Between Clinical Notes and Structured Tables in Electronic Health Records
f36f705960b15f803829a8b7.excerpt: arXiv:2605.26463v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Data consistency between unstructured clinical notes and structured tables in Electronic Health Records (EHRs) is essential for patient safety and clinical decision-making. However, existing work on note-table consistency verification mainly relies on surface-level matching of numeric values or simple events. Such approaches fail to capture the reasoning underlying real-world EHR documentation, including clinical interpretation, event relations, and temporal changes. To address this gap, we introduce EHR-ReasonCon, a reasoning-intensive benchmark for note-table consistency verification. Built on MIMIC-III with expert-guided annotations, it comprises 8,042 entities derived from clinical notes and provides high-quality ground-truth labels. The annotation protocol is supported by specialized table-exploration tools to ensure systematic evidence retrieval and reliable consistency assessment. We also propose EHR-INSPECTOR, an LLM-based framework that segments notes, extracts anchor entities and temporal references, and uses table-exploration tools to verify consistency against structured tables. Evaluated using expert-validated LLM-as-a-judge metrics under harsh and lenient criteria, EHR-INSPECTOR achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple model backbones. Analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness of its components and highlight differences from human verification. The code and dataset are available at https

163b191b638f33023dfdb33b.title_original: Personalized to Persuade: The Effects of Contextualization and Warmth on Trust and Reliance in Conversational AI
163b191b638f33023dfdb33b.excerpt: arXiv:2605.31275v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Contextualization is a form of personalization in which the message is framed in a context meaningful to the recipient, using their interests and background. Personalization is a known persuasive strategy of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in politics and marketing. However, the persuasive effect of contextualization in everyday tasks, where users often lack prior knowledge, remains unclear. We ran a $2\times2$ between-subjects experiment ($N = 407$) in a fictional scenario where participants had no prior opinions or knowledge. We examined how contextualization, combined with conversational warmth, shapes the persuasive power of an AI assistant arguing against expert recommendations and users' reliance on it. Our findings show that the neutral, non-contextualized assistant was the most persuasive. Contextualization and warmth each reduced persuasiveness on their own, but their interaction increased it. Reliance was present in all conditions, and neither cue changed it detectably. Trust predicted persuasion and reliance, yet neither contextualization nor warmth had an indirect effect through trust. Participants with higher self-reported AI literacy relied more on the assistant without trusting it more. Our study extends AI personalization research from political opinions to everyday decisions made without prior knowledge. The results suggest that users are more likely to be persuaded by, and defer to, an AI assista

52be56cdca44899c99890100.title_original: An Open Book, On Whose Terms? Power Dynamics in Sensor-Derived, LLM-Generated Summaries Sharing Between Older Adults and Remote Families
52be56cdca44899c99890100.excerpt: arXiv:2606.03876v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As older adults (OAs) increasingly favor aging in place, remote family members (RFMs) need meaningful awareness of their loved ones without intrusive monitoring. Large language models can provide rich interpretations of non-intrusive sensing data, yet recent work has largely emphasized technical accuracy over how families use or benefit from this information. We conducted formative interviews with 12 RFMs and 2 OAs, followed by a three-month deployment case study with one OA-RFM dyad. Our system provided daily AI-generated summaries of multimodal sensing data, which we iteratively refined with both parties using a research-through-design approach. Although the summaries integrated well into the dyad's daily routine, sustaining over 90% engagement, their lived experience revealed evolving tensions around agency, reassurance, privacy, trust, and communication, shaped by sensor limitations and existing communication misalignments. Our findings inform the design of future AI-mediated sharing systems that account for real-world sensing constraints and complex family care dynamics.

f18ad9e8dacc1a5dfd75dd50.title_original: LLMCodec: Adapting Video Codecs for Efficient Weight Compression of Large Language Models
f18ad9e8dacc1a5dfd75dd50.excerpt: arXiv:2606.05861v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rapid development of large language models(LLMs) has led to remarkable advances in natural language processing. However, the increasing scale of these models introduces substantial challenges in terms of storage, transmission, and deployment. Though great efforts have been devoted to model compression and quantization, existing methods often rely on fine-tuning or calibration data, which exhibit limited generalization across different tensor types. In this paper, we argue that video codecs offer a promising solution for LLM compression, due to their inherent compatibility with matrix structured data, configurable compression strategies, and the availability of highly optimized, off-the-shelf implementations. Therefore, we present LLMCodec, a video codec-based LLM compression method that integrates affine quantization with the recent VVC/H.266 video codec. Beyond VVC, we further compare a range of video codecs and encoding profiles to evaluate their impact on compression performance. Experiments on different models demonstrate the robustness and generality of LLMCodec. Notably, on LLaMA-3-8B at 2-bit precision, LLMCodec reduces perplexity by over 1.5x and improves downstream task accuracy by 21% compared with the existing method.

b5bd709596da3561c383645a.title_original: How Deep Are Deep GPs, Really? A Sharp Threshold and a Non-Gaussian Limit for Compositional GPs
b5bd709596da3561c383645a.excerpt: arXiv:2606.08218v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Compositional priors describe the generic properties of layered functions in deep Bayesian models, where deep neural networks with random weights are a canonical example. In the wide-network limit, the prior is a Gaussian process (GP) with a depth-dependent kernel, and its behaviour as depth grows has been extensively studied through this kernel. Here, we study another case, where each layer itself is a vector valued Gaussian process, and our aim is similarly to understand the limiting behaviour of the prior as depth grows. Previous GP work has established that for the radial basis function (RBF) kernel and a certain range of bandwidths $r$, the prior degenerates in the limit, converging to the set of constant functions, which is not useful as a probabilistic model. In this paper we establish several new results. First, we identify a sharp bandwidth threshold $r_c(d) = \Theta(\sqrt{d})$ above which the limit is degenerate, strengthening the earlier bounds. Second, and more importantly, we show that for $r$ below the threshold $r_c(d)$ the prior converges to a limit distribution $\pi_{\bar{Z}}$. We also prove that these distributions are non-degenerate and non-Gaussian, with non-vanishing dependence between coordinates. In contrast to the previously known degenerate regime, deep Gaussian process priors can therefore admit non-trivial limits. Empirically, we verify the threshold across a range of dimensions $d$, and demo

928c13ccbcc322b00600d4ee.title_original: Accounting for Purchased Artificial Intelligence Inference in Corporate Greenhouse Gas Inventories: A Token-Based Method
928c13ccbcc322b00600d4ee.excerpt: arXiv:2606.10660v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Purchased artificial intelligence (AI) inference belongs in Scope 3 Category 1 of a corporate greenhouse gas inventory, yet practice omits it or applies a spend-based factor that gives 1.7 to 12.3 times the physical estimate and cannot tell one model or region from another. This paper sets out a token-based method and open dataset: a cradle-to-gate boundary, four tiers of activity data, an effective-token basis, a four-term factor (serving electricity, embodied hardware, data-centre construction, disclosed final training runs) and a rule resolving any model identifier and region to a factor. Inference footprints span twelve times between model classes and nine between regions. The mid-class factor, 0.039 kg of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) per million billed tokens at the world-average grid, is the low end of a stated structural range: a less efficient serving configuration raises it 2.8 times, and replacing the training term with all model development, on its own boundary, gives 1.5 to 2.9 times it. Input bands alone give -18% to +29%. Published per-query energy estimates that can describe a mid-class model are 2.4 to 7.2 times the mid-class energy, above its structural range in four of five rows; those that can describe a frontier-class model bracket it at 0.7 to 1.6 times. Worked examples give 8.5 kg CO2e a year for a 200-person firm, and 2.1 tonnes for fifty developers using agentic coding tools on a mid-class m

80dbf058be76e44fa81cf460.title_original: Grammar-Constrained Decoding Can Jailbreak LLMs into Generating Malicious Code
80dbf058be76e44fa81cf460.excerpt: arXiv:2606.11817v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code generation, raising concerns that they may be misused to produce malicious code. Meanwhile, Grammar-Constrained Decoding (GCD) has been widely adopted to improve the reliability of LLM-generated code by enforcing syntactic validity. In this paper, we reveal a counterintuitive risk: this reliability-oriented technique can itself become an attack surface. We uncover a new jailbreak attack, termed CodeSpear, that exploits GCD to induce LLMs into generating malicious code. Our experiments show that simply applying a benign code grammar constraint can effectively jailbreak LLMs. To address this vulnerability, we propose CodeShield, a safety alignment approach that robustly preserves safe behavior even under attacker-controlled grammar constraints. CodeShield aligns the model in the code modality by teaching it to generate honeypot code under GCD. Such code is semantically harmless, so it does not implement the malicious request, and structurally diverse, so it is difficult to suppress through grammar tightening. At the same time, CodeShield still preserves natural-language refusals when natural language is available. Experiments on 10 popular LLMs across 4 benchmarks show that CodeSpear outperforms representative jailbreak baselines and increases the attack success rate by more than 30 percentage points on average. CodeShield also restores safety under CodeSpear wh

420fcd02294af1bace796ec2.title_original: DuoBench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Bimanual Manipulation in Simulation and the Real World
420fcd02294af1bace796ec2.excerpt: arXiv:2606.11901v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bimanual robot systems substantially expand manipulation capabilities, but coordinating two arms introduces additional control complexity and failure modes that are not well captured by existing benchmarks. We introduce DuoBench, an extensible benchmarking framework for bimanual manipulation policies on the FR3 Duo platform. DuoBench comprises eleven tasks spanning four coordination categories, implemented in simulation and partially replicated in the real world through reproducible task recipes with 3D-printable assets. In addition, we propose a stage-based evaluation scheme that supports fine-grained semantic failure analysis beyond binary success. It includes stage-conditional pass rates with confidence intervals as well as human-teleoperated datasets for all benchmark tasks. We benchmark several imitation-learning and vision-language-action policies in simulation and on real hardware. Our results show that current policies remain challenged by bimanual manipulation, particularly at the beginning of interaction, during parallel arm execution, and in sim-to-real transfer settings. We further find that simulation reveals the same failure modes as real-world experiments. DuoBench provides a reproducible testbed for analyzing them and studying future methods for dual-arm policy learning. Code, datasets, and videos are available at https://duobench.github.io

1d1ca5c5c35c47cef3a55d61.title_original: Robust Learning under Non-Gaussian Noise with Adaptive Log-Correntropy Loss
1d1ca5c5c35c47cef3a55d61.excerpt: arXiv:2606.16050v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robust deep learning under heavy-tailed and impulsive noise remains challenging because conventional losses such as mean squared error (MSE) exhibit unbounded sensitivity to outliers. Although correntropy-based objectives improve robustness, many conventional formulations rely on fixed kernel parameters that must be empirically tuned and remain static during training. To address these limitations, we propose an Adaptive Log-Correntropy Loss (ALCL), a heavy-tailed loss formulation that adaptively learns its robustness geometry during optimization. ALCL introduces a logarithmic residual model whose shape and scale parameters are learned jointly with network weights through differentiable reparameterization. This yields a heavy-tailed robust optimization objective whose psi-function is formally bounded and redescending, allowing the loss geometry to adapt dynamically to evolving residual statistics while suppressing extreme outliers. Comparative experiments on four widely used benchmark datasets spanning grayscale and red-green-blue (RGB) image data under mixed heavy-tailed and impulsive noise demonstrate that ALCL consistently outperforms MSE and optimally tuned generalized correntropy losses in both reconstruction fidelity and downstream classification accuracy. While performance differences remain small under low-noise conditions, under high-noise regimes ALCL improves median accuracy by up to 4.75% on grayscale benchm

ff0a992ebf0473d4ba323e76.title_original: First-Token Broadcasters: Mechanistic Origins of Language Identity and Distributed Robustness in Transformers
ff0a992ebf0473d4ba323e76.excerpt: arXiv:2606.22361v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How is language identity represented and causally maintained in transformers, and to what extent do the mechanisms identified in one language set transfer to other languages and training regimes? We introduce Language Identity Head Ablation (LIHA), a causal intervention that zeros each attention head individually and measures the resulting language switch rate. Across our multilingual evaluation sets, LIHA identifies heads whose ablation has disproportionate effects on output language. In GPT-2, a small set of first-token broadcaster heads---led by L6H1 (switch rate 0.32, 3.23$\sigma$ above the population mean)---attend persistently to the first prompt token across query positions. The combination of persistent first-token attention and causal sensitivity suggests that these heads participate in maintaining output language. Following ablation, first-token attention increases in heads above the ablated layer for the ablations tested (permutation test against random five-head sets, $p < 10^{-5}$). We do not test whether these heads functionally compensate for the ablated head. We also compare Qwen2.5-1.5B-Base and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, which are matched in architecture and parameter count but differ in training history. The base model is nearly flat (max SR$=$0.016, 200/336 heads at SR$=$0.0), whereas the instruct model concentrates causal influence at layer~0, led by L0H5 (SR$=$0.224, 8.93$\sigma$ above the mean). Fina

ccf575e4a3397f2ca0899bb7.title_original: Neglected Free Lunch from Post-training: Progress Advantage for LLM Agents
ccf575e4a3397f2ca0899bb7.excerpt: arXiv:2606.26080v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Process reward models enable fine-grained, step-level evaluation of LLMs, yet building them for agentic settings remains prohibitively difficult: long-horizon interactions, irreversible actions, and stochastic environment feedback make both human annotation and Monte Carlo estimation infeasible at scale. In this work, we show that reinforcement learning (RL) post-training already provides the ingredients for effective step-level scoring, eliminating the need for dedicated reward model training altogether. Concretely, we derive an implicit advantage under a general stochastic Markov decision process, which we term progress advantage -- log-probability ratio between the RL-trained policy and its reference policy exactly recovers the optimal advantage function. This formulation makes the resulting signal annotation-free, domain-agnostic, and available as a byproduct of the standard RL post-training pipeline. We validate the effectiveness of the progress advantage across three different applications: test-time scaling, uncertainty quantification, and failure attribution on five benchmarks and four model families. Across all settings, it consistently outperforms confidence-based baselines and, despite requiring no task-specific training, surpasses dedicated trained reward models. We complement these results with deeper analyses on characteristics of progress advantage, offering practical guidance for adoption in real-world

a73254d6ed27353a4a24d2cd.title_original: DPPE: Rethinking Camera-Based Positional Encoding for Scaling Multi-View Transformers
a73254d6ed27353a4a24d2cd.excerpt: arXiv:2606.31585v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The remarkable scalability of Transformers has expanded their application to 3D computer vision, where camera-aware positional encoding is crucial for providing spatial cues in multi-view geometry. Recent advancements have established the practice of using camera parameters---such as extrinsics or projection matrices---as relative positional encoding into the query, key, and value vectors of the attention mechanism. However, when scaling up the training recipe of novel view synthesis (NVS) models with the camera-based positional encoding, we observe a significant issue: model performance stagnates in the late stages of training. In this paper, we investigate the cause of the performance bottleneck when scaling up and demonstrate that storing rotation and translation given by the positional encoding in the same dimensions of the value vector causes indeterminacy in their independent identification, hindering training scalability. To address this, we propose Decoupled Pose Positional Encoding (DPPE), a novel camera-based positional encoding that explicitly decouples rotation and translation. Extensive evaluations on NVS tasks demonstrate that DPPE enables stable long-term training even in scaled-up training setup. Furthermore, it exhibits superior generalization performance in extrapolation settings, such as handling an increased number of viewpoints and zoom-in scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/sbintuit

4d0f13604a195222934759cc.title_original: From Solvers to Research: Large Language Model-Driven Formal Mathematics at the Research Frontier
4d0f13604a195222934759cc.excerpt: arXiv:2607.07779v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent developments in AI for Mathematics (AI4Math), especially Large Language Model (LLM)-driven theorem provers, has achieved remarkable success in formal proof generation for well-defined mathematical problems through Interactive Theorem Proving (ITP) languages. However, current systems remain fundamentally limited in tackling frontier research mathematics, such as discovering new theorems or resolving open conjectures, which are often open-ended, under-specified, and involve multiple layers of abstraction. We argue that the next leap in AI4Math systems requires a decisive shift from predefined problem-solvers to research agents that can address frontier mathematical challenges with rigorous formal mathematical reasoning. In this position paper, we provide a systematic review of the field, covering datasets, auto-formalization, and proof synthesis. More importantly, we identify core limitations of existing systems in serving as mathematical research agents, examining issues across datasets, relational structure, mathematical exploration, tool ecosystem, and human-AI collaboration, outlining a strategic road-map for the future of AI4Math.

75fb5c96b05755399f04a3a1.title_original: CLAP: Direct VLM-to-VLA Adaptation via Language-Action Grounding
75fb5c96b05755399f04a3a1.excerpt: arXiv:2607.08974v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit semantic capabilities from pretrained VLMs, yet large-scale post-training on robot data and architectural modifications can reshape the backbone so extensively that it becomes difficult to isolate what the VLM contributes to control. Directly converting pretrained VLMs into VLAs with minimal architectural change offers a more transparent path to understanding how VLM capabilities transfer across model scales. The core obstacle is output-distribution mismatch: predicting actions as bare numeric token sequences moves generation away from the VLM's pretrained language distribution, degrading the capabilities we seek to preserve. To address this, we propose CLAP (Causal Language-Action Prediction), which prepends each numeric action sequence with a natural-language action description, causally conditioning precise action-token prediction on a language-action plan without modifying the backbone architecture. With only 4-5 hours of training, 2B CLAP achieves 90.8% on LIBERO (+14.9 pt over VLA-0) and improves robustness on LIBERO-PRO under language, object, and spatial perturbations. Ablations attribute the gains to action-grounded language semantics, and on a real UR5e robot 2B CLAP reaches 60% success against 15% for matched VLA-0. We release CLAP at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B as an open-weight, multi-scale compact VLA family from a single VLM lineage, enabling controlled analysis of VLM-t

739411915378860a0dde308d.title_original: Multi-Axis Max@K Reinforcement Learning for Representative Diversity in Text-to-Image Generation
739411915378860a0dde308d.excerpt: arXiv:2607.14962v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models produce realistic, prompt-aligned images, but samples for the same prompt often cover only a few visually distinct modes. For person-centric prompts, this lack of diversity can reflect or amplify demographic skew. We formalize representative diversity as target-mode coverage: how well a set of samples covers predefined modes, such as colors or perceived-race categories. We then propose MultiMaxPO, a reinforcement learning post-training method that improves this coverage in diffusion T2I models by optimizing a multi-axis max@K objective. Given one score per mode for each sample, multi-axis max@K takes the maximum over samples for each mode and then sums these maxima. A sample therefore receives credit for a mode only when it raises that mode's maximum, so different samples are rewarded for different modes. We verify this credit assignment on a synthetic Gaussian mixture and on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium with pixel-based color rewards, and then apply it to perceived-appearance fairness. On held-out prompts and under three automatic evaluators, MultiMaxPO improves the Fairness Score over the base model by 0.22-0.36 on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and by 0.07-0.19 on FLUX.1-dev, outperforms matched RL baselines, and maintains image quality and text alignment. Code is available at https://github.com/KuOnoda/multi-axis-maxk.

fe026bcf2531b5f3ef348790.title_original: Closing the Lab-to-Store Gap: A Data-Efficient Post-Training and Experience-Driven Learning VLA Framework for Retail Humanoids
fe026bcf2531b5f3ef348790.excerpt: arXiv:2607.20345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Closing the gap between benchmark performance and reliable real-world operation remains a central challenge for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) humanoid robots, which must handle execution errors, distribution shifts, and environmental variability. This paper presents DEED (Data-Efficient Post-Training and Experience-Driven Learning), a systems-level approach evaluated on a supermarket chip-restocking task using a Unitree G1-Edu humanoid robot and the GR00T N1.6 foundation model. DEED comprises three key components: (1) a data-efficient post-training pipeline with control-frequency alignment, data curation, task-relevant visual highlighting, and reduced VLA dependence; (2) a real-world study of experience-driven refinement, adapted from RECAP via a text-based advantage prefix and a vision-language value function; and (3) a latent-space analysis tool for studying in- and out-of-distribution behavior. Our results suggest that bridging the lab-to-store gap is primarily a systems integration challenge rather than an architectural one: careful data design and targeted post-training can transform a policy that fails under naive fine-tuning into a competent real-world system using only a single GPU.

ae68aa6dfb3f35e7e2a5878d.title_original: Automated Numerical Stability Analysis of Deep Learning Operators
ae68aa6dfb3f35e7e2a5878d.excerpt: arXiv:2607.25494v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Finite-precision arithmetic unavoidably introduces numerical approximation errors. Numerical computations may use insufficient precision or an improper formulation, which leads to numerical instability. In this paper, we introduce a unified software tool for stochastic numerical validation of deep-learning operators. The tool follows CESTAC on supported exposed operations and uses an operator-level data-perturbation approximation for GEMM-like kernels. Our developed software not only enables numerical validation with a single computation pass but also detects the sources of numerical instability and provides numerical stability monitoring during deep learning training and inference. We verified its effectiveness on the detection of polluted operators with injected numerical instabilities across various tasks. We believe that our developed method and tools provide valuable insights into developing numerically stable computing kernels, which are particularly critical for numerically stable and efficient deep learning training and inference.

40bf19e66e684ec11450c80e.title_original: Same Illness, Different Voice: Clinical Language Models Lose Accuracy When Patients Speak for Themselves
40bf19e66e684ec11450c80e.excerpt: arXiv:2607.27384v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Clinical language models are evaluated on vignettes written in a clinician's voice, but patients describe the same illness in their own. We pair 1,000 MedQA cases with three audited retellings (clinical, socioeconomic, cultural) and test 12 open models. Every model is less accurate when the patient speaks in a marked voice, by 9.6 points on average (95% CI 8.2 to 11.0), with no detectable shrinkage at larger scale. Matched controls trace the penalty. Generation temperature does not explain it, a plain first-person paraphrase that states every fact accounts for 2.4 points, and attaching the original vignette to the marked narrative recovers 7.0. We read this mainly as a failure to use facts expressed in patients' own words, not as a reaction to social cues, although our voices bundle both. Chain-of-thought and explicit debiasing instructions together close about a fifth of the gap. Having the same model first restate the account as a clinical vignette halves it and raises marked-voice accuracy by 3.9 points, whereas a structured-schema pipeline closes the same gap but is 7.1 points less accurate than the rewrite. Rewriting also invents plausible details, which we quantify. Code, data and analysis scripts: https://github.com/prabhjotschugh/narrativeshield-sdoh-medqa

5c5a767d4aed616c2ac51b87.title_original: Dense Language Generation Made Simple: Deterministic, Randomized, and Multi-Order Algorithms
5c5a767d4aed616c2ac51b87.excerpt: arXiv:2608.01320v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language generation in the limit is a theoretical framework for studying how a generator can learn to produce new valid strings from a stream of positive examples. In this model, an adversary chooses an unknown language from a countable family and enumerates its elements in an arbitrary order, while the generator must eventually output only elements of the language that have not yet appeared in the enumeration. Reliable generation is thus formalized through two eventual guarantees: validity and novelty relative to the observed data. To further quantify the breadth of the generator's outputs, Kleinberg and Wei (FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) introduced lower density as a measure of output coverage. Given an order representing the importance or relevance of possible outputs, lower density is the asymptotic lower bound, as $n$ grows, on the fraction of the first $n$ elements of the target language that the generator outputs before they appear in the data. Kleinberg and Wei showed that $1/2$ is the optimal lower-density guarantee for deterministic algorithms. We develop a simple and unified framework for obtaining optimal lower-density guarantees. We first give a deterministic algorithm that recovers the optimal guarantee of $1/2$ with a significantly simpler analysis than prior work. We then demonstrate the flexibility of our framework through two extensions. First, against an oblivious adversary, randomization raises the optimal

60f8cfd5be5dab802d4a7cb1.title_original: How Far from Clinical Deployment? Evaluating the Complete Unsupervised Domain Adaptation Pipeline in Medical Imaging
60f8cfd5be5dab802d4a7cb1.excerpt: arXiv:2608.12035v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deploying unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) in clinical practice requires choosing which algorithm to use and which of its trained models to ship. However, the deployment (target) domain is unlabeled, so models cannot be evaluated directly on it, leaving it unclear which to select. We address this by evaluating the complete UDA pipeline, considering both adaptation and label-free selection together. Our study covers eleven clinically relevant cross-domain scenarios from nine medical imaging datasets, with ten UDA algorithms and 13 label-free selection methods (validators), evaluating over 80,000 trained models in total. By this, we find that a capable adapted model usually exists, but identifying it without target labels is difficult: the validator-selected models leave a large and structural target performance gap to the best available one, with no evaluated validator consistently reliable. Towards closing it, we explore two strategies, ensembling and a small target-labeling budget; both narrow this gap but do not close it entirely. Overall, deployable UDA depends on the complete pipeline; addressing the less explored selection step could bring much of current UDA closer to clinical use. Our code is open sourced at \href{https://xiongyiheng.github.io/complete-uda-pipeline-site/}{Project Page}.

677db1924fcd1349b1a7220f.title_original: Import What You Need: Learning When and How to Augment EHR Graphs with External Knowledge
677db1924fcd1349b1a7220f.excerpt: arXiv:2609.01839v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Longitudinal prediction from electronic health records (EHRs) is limited by the sparsity and irregularity in patient trajectories, and knowledge augmentation with external knowledge graphs (KGs) offers a promising way to alleviate these issues. However, KG expansion often follows predefined rules, with limited control over whether and how to augment each visit as a patient's state evolves. We propose ReTA, a Reinforcement learning-based dynamic Topology Augmentation framework that casts KG import as a per-visit, budget-aware policy. ReTA first constructs an offline refined pool of KG-grounded templates, then learns a policy to select one augment action per visit from three options: Soft Import, which enriches node features without modifying graph topology, Hard Import, which grafts a compact KG subgraph onto the visit graph to create message-passing shortcuts, and Skip, which leaves the visit unaugmented when the base encoder is already confident. To stabilize learning, ReTA employs a decoupled encoder that processes semantic and structural signals in separate channels and fuses them via adaptive gating. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV across diagnosis prediction, mortality, and readmission show that ReTA consistently outperforms strong baselines while remaining efficient, with larger gains under sparse supervision. ReTA transfers across datasets and knowledge graphs and yields interpretable augmentation patterns

d13aac8fb6cd81b9bbfd7ff3.title_original: Diffusion models for eye-gaze trajectory generation using position and velocity representations
d13aac8fb6cd81b9bbfd7ff3.excerpt: arXiv:2609.05522v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Eye-tracking data are expensive to collect, requiring specialized hardware and controlled laboratory conditions, and difficult to share due to privacy regulations, which together limit the quantity and diversity of gaze data available for research. We investigate unconditional gaze generation using diffusion models in position and component-wise velocity representations. The models are trained and evaluated on eight-second visual-search trajectories from 28 participants, using a split of 23 training participants and five held-out validation participants, with three training seeds. Evaluation includes kinematic distributions, trajectory geometry, event statistics, and a temporal Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty as a learned comparator. Across eight position-derived features, mean Jensen-Shannon divergence is $0.016 \pm 0.004$ for the position model and $0.037 \pm 0.002$ for the velocity model, with standard deviations calculated across training seeds. These scores do not establish that representation choice caused the difference. A separate comparison using the same evaluation method shows that the ordering of the models varies across training seeds. The position model also produces smaller feature discrepancies than a kinematic Markov baseline. Differences in saccade counts between real and generated data depend strongly on the velocity threshold used to detect events. The results provide quantitative reference me

e0bf14a9b9457486d6498edb.title_original: CleanVideo: Adaptive Concept Erasure for Text-to-Video Diffusion Models
e0bf14a9b9457486d6498edb.excerpt: arXiv:2609.20267v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Concept erasure aims to selectively eliminate undesired visual semantics from pre-trained generative models without compromising their general utility. Extending concept erasure from images to video is nontrivial. Target concepts emerge gradually and vary across frames and denoising steps. As a result, fixed interventions may miss the target or introduce blurring, jitter, and content distortion. We propose CleanVideo, a selective erasure framework that performs low-dimensional subspace intervention controlled by a tri-modal gating mechanism. By jointly processing spatiotemporal visual features, timestep signals, and textual semantics, CleanVideo determines where, when, and whether to intervene, steering erased content toward natural surrogate concepts when such surrogates can be clearly defined while preserving non-target content. Experiments on three video diffusion models show that CleanVideo effectively erases target concepts while maintaining visual fidelity and temporal coherence, outperforming existing baselines under frame-level and video-level evaluations and under concept-recovery attacks when the protected pipeline remains intact.

b22d94d7f5b9b1f516e6209c.title_original: Forecasting Brain Tracer Distribution from Pre-Contrast MRI: A Comparison of Direct Regression and Flow Matching
b22d94d7f5b9b1f516e6209c.excerpt: arXiv:2609.22377v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The brain fluid clearance system can be studied with intrathecal contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). By injecting a tracer into the spinal canal and performing MRI over 24--48\,h, one can measure how a tracer injected into the cerebrospinal fluid spreads through the brain. As this is an invasive procedure requiring several MRI scans, we ask how much of the later tracer distribution can be predicted from the pre-contrast scan and elapsed time alone. Using 104 training patients (878 MRI volumes), we compared a direct image-to-image regression model with a more complex generative model based on conditional flow matching, and tested both on 23 held-out patients and on 51 patients from a separate cohort with idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH). Relative to simply copying the pre-contrast scan, the direct model reduced the mean absolute error (intensities normalized to $[0,1]$) from 0.089 to 0.036, about 60\%, in held-out patients and from 0.075 to 0.056, about 25\%, in the iNPH cohort. The reduction held in every sampled elapsed-time interval and brain compartment, and errors remained largest at 20--30\,h and in the ventricles, where enhancement is strongest. Its predicted change maps agreed with the observed tracer enhancement rather than only reproducing anatomy. The generative model was less accurate in both cohorts. A substantial part of the later tracer distribution is therefore predictable

c48863f56b775193bc514cfe.title_original: Bayesian Optimization with Fisher Information Geometry: Gradient Bounds and Trust-Region Methods
c48863f56b775193bc514cfe.excerpt: arXiv:2609.31107v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study Bayesian optimization (BO) through the lens of information geometry. Pulling back the Fisher information metric through the surrogate posterior map yields a local sensitivity tensor on the input space, which leads to an upper bound on the gradient of reparameterizable acquisition functions (AFs). This view explains vanishing-gradient behavior in high-dimensional BO and provides a common interpretation of heuristics such as RAASP and dimension-scaled lengthscales. The upper bound can also serve as a generic recipe to understand the behavior of new acquisition functions or surrogates in high input dimensions as well. Using the bounds, we also identify necessary conditions for an input location to be an optimizer of the AF for a univariate Gaussian predictive posterior. Building on this analysis, we propose FITR, a trust-region-based BO method that replaces lengthscale-based scaling with local pullback-Fisher weights. FITR is not restricted to GP kernels with explicit lengthscales and easily generalizes to non-isotropic surrogates. FITR shows competitive performance on several benchmarks.

04683ae3535e920351907816.title_original: Bayesian Active Learning for Intent Disambiguation in Interactive Robot Planning
04683ae3535e920351907816.excerpt: arXiv:2609.34270v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interactive robot planning requires robots to infer and execute human intentions from natural language instructions that are often ambiguous, incomplete, or underspecified. Although large language models (LLMs) provide a powerful interface for clarification, relying on the generative model to drive an multi-turn conversation can introduce systematic failures. We propose a Bayesian framework that treats clarification as an active learning problem over grounded Signal Temporal Logic (STL) task specifications. Our method uses LLMs to initialize candidate formal specifications and translate informative contrasts into natural-language clarification questions, while Bayesian optimization maintains uncertainty estimation over user intent and selects queries that maximize information gain. After convergence, the inferred STL specification is passed to a formal planner to synthesize a verifiable robot trajectory. Across four simulated and real-world task domains, our approach generally achieves higher task satisfaction and requires fewer clarification rounds than LLM baselines, while helping smaller models close the performance gap against larger reasoning models.

4d2f1319f02657c26e95bcb2.title_original: A Systematic Analysis of the Predictive Power of LM Surprisal in Reading Chinese
4d2f1319f02657c26e95bcb2.excerpt: arXiv:2610.04898v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This study analyzes the predictive power of LM-derived, token-level surprisal on Mandarin Chinese reading times. Using a suite of Chinese-Pythia models (14M--1.4B) trained from scratch with 30B tokens, we examine how well surprisal predicts first fixation duration, gaze duration, and total reading time in three paragraph-level eye-tracking corpora of Mandarin Chinese (GECO-CN, HKP, and MECO). Contrary to previous null findings, our results show that surprisal is predictive of Chinese reading times. However, whether predictive power scales with model size and the amount of training is corpus-specific: bigger models predict reading times better in GECO-CN, whereas inverse scaling emerges in HKP and, at the largest sizes, in MECO. Subsequently, we find that checkpoints whose surprisal remains closer to $n$-gram statistics are better predictors of reading in HKP and MECO, providing one possible explanation for the inverse scaling behavior. All in all, the predictive power of surprisal on Chinese reading time measurements is corpus-specific, which cautions against drawing conclusions about language model scale from a single corpus.

651567889cc8aa02942c0b6d.title_original: CausalBind: Causal Modeling and Learning for Protein-Molecule Virtual Screening
651567889cc8aa02942c0b6d.excerpt: arXiv:2610.07340v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Protein-molecule virtual screening is increasingly cast as a problem of representation learning in a shared embedding space. Existing methods rely on dense holistic alignment, entangling invariant binding determinants with nuisance correlations and limiting transfer to new targets. Binding in protein-molecule systems involves sparse cross-modality interactions: binding is governed by a small contact interface and a few decisive local interactions (e.g., hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, and salt bridges) rather than the global structures of the protein and molecule. We hypothesize that uncovering and leveraging sparse interaction patterns is critical for generalization beyond the training data, as these patterns are reusable and expected to improve performance across different scenarios. Since the training data contain only observed binding pairs, we formalize this prior via a V-structure causal model under Heckman-style selection, and establish three theoretical results: (i) when the compatibility between concepts is bilinear, the latent concepts of interacting proteins and molecules are not identifiable, even if the interaction is sparse; (ii) with a non-bilinear compatibility function, these concepts and their sparse interaction support are component-wise identifiable under a sparse antichain condition; and (iii) a low-rank relaxation yields subspace identifiability of the interaction modes, and applies to bilin

1586bc4ba8dfc134c4eec510.title_original: Disentangling Dual Image References in Frequency Aware Diffusion Models for Personalized Generation
1586bc4ba8dfc134c4eec510.excerpt: arXiv:2610.07684v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Personalized image generation aims to synthesize text-driven images conditioned on reference images, while mainly casting the generation as image customization for foreground and style transfer for background. Previous arts of diffusion models suffers from the text misalignment with background for image customization and foreground for style transfer during the denoising process. Such facts, as we observed, rooted from the entanglement among hybrid frequency bands during the denoising process. In particular, the low-frequency band primarily captures color information, mid-frequency band encodes global structure, while high-frequency band corresponds to local texture. Besides, the early (high-noise) denoising stage mainly focuses on the low-and-mid frequency bands, while the late (low-noise) denoising stage progressively exhibits the high-frequency band, which, all together, overwhelm the text prompt guidance, suffering from the heavy reliance on reference image. To address such salient limitation, in this paper, we study personalized generation based on dual references - customization and color style reference - to propose a paradigm to disentangle these Dual image references within Frequency-aware Diffusion Models, dubbed Dual-FDM, to simultaneously tackle two crucial personalized image generation tasks: customization style transfer and color style transfer, by disentangling different frequency bands via mask strategy

1af6bfa775cc78bb8cdb68b6.title_original: Shared Geometry As A Rosetta Stone: Cross-Modal Alignment Without Paired Data
1af6bfa775cc78bb8cdb68b6.excerpt: arXiv:2610.09411v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal representations enable zero-shot classification and retrieval, but aligning independently trained models usually requires large amounts of paired data. Yet, the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that models trained on different modalities may converge spontaneously toward a shared representation geometry. But then, do we even need paired examples for cross-modal alignment? Remarkably, we show that paired examples are unnecessary for coarse cross-modal alignment. Our simple Wasserstein Procrustes method with a coarse geometric initialization (GeoWarP) aligns two disjoint embedding sets by estimating a single orthogonal map without seeing any pairs. Across datasets, modalities, and unimodal models, we show that we can consistently align independently trained representations without pairs, and standard geometric alignment metrics accurately predict when this is possible. Nevertheless, we can naturally benefit from paired examples. In the very few-pair regime, our method substantially outperforms existing ones, while staying competitive with pair-based methods with more added examples. Finally, we demonstrate that the resulting alignments can enable text-to-image generation without paired examples. These results show that independently trained models often share enough geometry to establish cross-modal correspondence with little or no paired data.

71027097db7549ebc60d884a.title_original: Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines
71027097db7549ebc60d884a.excerpt: arXiv:2610.15897v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Qwen3-8B reviewing Llama-3.1-8B in math adds 33.2 points, yet Qwen3-8B alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the result. Reviewing another model's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator. We show that this confuses verification, which adds accuracy beyond either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer supplies answers it could have given on its own. Measured against the stronger model alone, across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code and reasoning, review beats it in only 9 of 96 review directions, and does worse the larger the capability gap. The reason is anchoring: the reviewer mostly follows the generator, discarding its own correct answers. Review costs 2.6 to 2.8 times as much as the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper. Studies of verification should report the stronger model alone, not only the gain over the generator.

b408e5ea169f2d5c0dfe5b90.title_original: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
b408e5ea169f2d5c0dfe5b90.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17697v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify an

38734d4172c922faf92b52ef.title_original: TStruct: Learning Shared Temporal Structures for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
38734d4172c922faf92b52ef.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17864v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-term time series forecasting requires learning temporal dependencies that remain stable and generalizable under temporal distribution shifts. However, real-world time series are often noisy, non-stationary, and heterogeneous, making deep learning models prone to overfitting incidental temporal interactions in the training data. This raises a question: when observations are difficult to align, could temporal relationships be easier to reuse? To investigate this possibility, we analyze patch-level temporal relationship matrices across commonly used time series datasets, revealing dominant patterns shared across different temporal windows and variables. Comparisons with patch-shuffled and IID Gaussian controls further support the presence of reusable temporal relationship structures. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textbf{T}emporal \textbf{Struct}ure Network (\textbf{TStruct}), a simple yet effective network that learns reusable temporal dependency structures and adaptively combines them for each sample and variable. Specifically, TStruct directly parameterizes a set of shared temporal dependency matrices and generates normalized combination weights using dynamic sample information and static variable priors. These weights represent a soft allocation of each sample-variable pair over shared temporal dependency structures, enabling the model to generate adaptive temporal dependency matrices under shared struc

2b0b42f2d351d32f087f30c3.title_original: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
2b0b42f2d351d32f087f30c3.excerpt: arXiv:2610.18877v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs, without explicitly requiring their representations to preserve how the underlying signals evolve. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in Lotus, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, Lotus achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that Lotus uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle

d681b7b7acc04f1d89529901.title_original: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
d681b7b7acc04f1d89529901.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21375v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent 'memory tokens' for a frozen LLM. Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM's input embedding space. Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering. Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108x fewer tokens to represent the source documents. Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent's past turns) increases throughout the trajectory. In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent's tendency to

e48e7db7e83cdfa7014c87a0.title_original: Scaling Graph Reasoning in Language Models with Learnable Graph Positional Encodings
e48e7db7e83cdfa7014c87a0.excerpt: arXiv:2610.27439v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings.

2d60ecbe0296c3fa84addcce.title_original: TPO: Tri-level Distributionally Robust Learning for OOD Direct Preference Optimization
2d60ecbe0296c3fa84addcce.excerpt: arXiv:2610.28229v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) minimizes empirical risk over observed preference comparisons, implicitly assuming that the training preference distribution matches the deployment preference distribution. In practice, this distributional assumption often fails, as preference distribution shifts can arise at three levels: group-level shift, prompt-level shift, and preference-level shift. Such multi-level distributional mismatch poses a critical challenge for safe LLM deployment, yet existing robust DPO methods typically either model uncertainty over the joint preference distribution or focus on individual sources of shift, leaving the hierarchical structure of OOD preference shifts underexplored. We propose TPO, a tri-level distributionally robust framework for OOD preference alignment, which jointly models all three levels of distributional uncertainty through a hierarchically structured rectangular ambiguity set. By instantiating it with Wasserstein distance, we derive a tractable and interpretable objective that combines a preference-level margin penalty, prompt-level adversarial embedding perturbation, and worst-case group reweighting, each governed by an independent radius. We establish finite-sample convergence guarantees and empirically validate the effectiveness of TPO across diverse OOD environments.

02de0679f9a656746e0f1e07.title_original: Fitting Conventional and Neural Exchange-Correlation Functionals to Accurate Densities without Self-Consistent Fields
02de0679f9a656746e0f1e07.excerpt: arXiv:2610.30022v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Exchange-correlation functionals are usually fitted with energy-only losses, so better energies often bring worse densities. We introduce a workflow that predicts in closed form, from one Fock build on inverse Kohn-Sham orbitals of any accurate density, a functional's self-consistent density, and fits it to that density with no self-consistent-field solution. Fitted convexly, a CF22D-form hybrid beats CF22D and MN15 on unseen energies, dipole moments, and unfitted densities (6.8- and 22-fold lower density error). A neural meta-GGA fitted to 6 energies and 11 densities beats SCAN in both.

a554055b3d248e432fae71c0.title_original: Mine or Yours? Self-Other Confusion in Latent LLM Communication
a554055b3d248e432fae71c0.excerpt: arXiv:2610.33020v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: If two minds were linked, would each still know which thoughts are its own? Language models are increasingly linked in this way: instead of exchanging text, one model reads another's key-value cache. Systems that join a foreign cache to the receiver's own use one of two layouts: the cache lies over the receiver's own context, at the same token positions, or in front of it. We give two copies of one model different private priorities and link them in both layouts. With the cache over its own context, the receiver gives a fact found only in its partner's cache in every answer. Yet in about half of its answers it gives the partner's priority as its own, in both Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B: as often as a receiver that ignored whose priority was whose, although the text in the cache names its owner. With the same cache moved in front, this falls to 5% in Qwen but only to 43% in Llama, although both models nearly stop naming the partner's priority as the one they are using. Where the cache sits matters, yet neither layout in use protects both models. Fewer such errors do not mean better attribution: once the cache is moved, the receiver names the partner's priority as the partner's less often, not more, and its report of an inserted memory cannot tell the partner's cache from a copy of its own. In short, shared caches deliver content but not ownership.

babf0e70e028c059c0bf8e76.title_original: The Price of Scale in Proactive Memory Recall
babf0e70e028c059c0bf8e76.excerpt: arXiv:2610.34507v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A long-lived assistant that brings up memories without being asked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption. We show that this decision is a multiple-testing problem whose difficulty grows with the store size N. On replays of LongMemEval, a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at N=8 reaches 84-100% at N=2048 across embedding models and cue types; LoCoMo and LLM judges show it too. We prove that a gate which thresholds the best of N independent irrelevant scores at false-alarm rate alpha operates at a per-item false-positive rate of about -ln(1-alpha)/N, which pins its hit rate to the far left of the ROC and makes it regularly varying in N under regular variation. Replayed hit rates stay within its bounds for mixed cues up to 0.3 points, and hit rates carry over to held-out questions to within 6.0 points. At matched false alarms the deployed score recalls 14-26 points more than raw cosine. A cue-swap conformal gate, which ranks the current cue among other cues on the same store, has a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability. With a background from the user's unfiltered history it keeps false alarms at 3-6% on LongMemEval at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold; on LoCoMo it overshoots or turns conservative depending on the source of its reference cues. In a chronological replay with the user's own earlier messages as references, it fires on 5-8% of q

d56731a77ebafd26ccb566cb.title_original: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
d56731a77ebafd26ccb566cb.excerpt: arXiv:2610.35532v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unsafe deserialization turns untrusted data into attacker-controlled execution, and a single vulnerability can admit diverse exploit variants that evade defenses tailored to a known exploit. Existing defenses typically operate at a single enforcement point with limited visibility into the full attack. Combining controls across layers offers complementary protection, but coordinating them to preserve legitimate functionality and adapting them to new variants requires substantial expert effort. We propose JANUS, a red-blue adversarial framework for automated cross-layer defense synthesis. Starting from a known exploit, \sys iteratively refines deployment-specific policies in an isolated offline environment. A black-box attacker probes the current policy for exploit variants using only externally observable feedback. The defender summarizes each verified variant into its security-relevant effects, uses counterfactual replay to separate complementary coverage from redundant enforcement, and jointly selects and scopes controls across layers. Each candidate policy is validated against accumulated exploits and benign workflows. We evaluate JANUS on sixteen vulnerability deployments across six Java and PHP applications against gateway, application, system, and cross-layer defenses. JANUS reduces held-out attack success to 6.2%, compared with 18.8-55.0% for the baselines, fully mitigates 13 of 16 deployments, and preserves 98.4

b453627db199b706a0828be2.title_original: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
b453627db199b706a0828be2.excerpt: arXiv:2610.35541v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Web services increasingly expose backend interfaces that let users delegate tasks to AI agents, which invoke service operations directly without navigating websites. This shift changes how existing Web vulnerabilities can be exploited. We investigate these changes through VELA, an executable benchmark covering 44 vulnerabilities across twelve Web application families. The benchmark preserves vulnerable backends and derives agent-facing interfaces from legitimate workflows. We evaluate three commercial agents across multiple interface configurations, using controlled comparisons to separate interface effects from agent behavior and independent oracles to verify attack outcomes. Our results show that the agent realizes every attack that direct interface invocation realizes in the reference configuration, so exploitability is set mainly by the interface: 91% of vulnerabilities remain exploitable under the reference design. Interface restrictions prevent some attacks by removing required operations or limiting input control, while retention remains high across vulnerability classes. No case-level loss in the reference configuration is attributed to agent refusal or input normalization, and in one case the agent completed an attack by supplying calls the attacker omitted. Across the tested configurations, interface design affects exploitability more than agent choice, moving retention from 39% to 95% against at most 4.5 poi
b453627db199b706a0828be2.title_ko: AI 에이전트 기반 웹 접근이 웹 취약점 공격에 미치는 영향 연구
b453627db199b706a0828be2.summary_ko: 본 연구는 사용자가 AI 에이전트를 통해 웹 서비스를 이용할 때 발생하는 취약점 공격 변화를 VELA 벤치마크를 통해 분석했습니다. 에이전트가 직접 웹 인터페이스를 조작하는 환경에서 기존 웹 취약점의 91%가 여전히 유효함을 확인했으며, 보안과 사용성 간의 설계 균형에 대한 통찰을 제공합니다.

curation.reason_ko: AI 에이전트 환경에서 기존 웹 취약점 공격의 91%가 여전히 유효함을 입증한 연구 결과

6c412f5623f569402c9ee437.title_original: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization for Agentic Robotics
6c412f5623f569402c9ee437.excerpt: arXiv:2610.35817v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra now directly control robots and can generalize better than vision-language-action models (VLAs). We argue that this ability could arise from two distinct, composable skills: semantic reasoning, to understand what a task asks for in a scene, and motion control, to move the robot to do it. We show that small open VLMs are already capable of the first and mainly lack the second. We introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches this missing motion skill, entirely in simulation on simple primitive tasks and from the model's own successes, with no frontier teacher or distillation and no real-world robot data. ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness while running 3x faster and 17x cheaper, and 74.0% on a bimanual adaptation of RoboLab-120, on par with GPT-6 Astra's 72.2%. ZAP also generalizes to new objects, goals, and strategies, and in simulation to a robot embodiment on which it never trained.

bb782a573d3feedd4edf9a7b.title_original: Full Collapse Is Suboptimal: Controlled Partial Neural Collapse for Long-Tailed Recognition
bb782a573d3feedd4edf9a7b.excerpt: arXiv:2610.36460v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent long-tailed recognition (LTR) methods incorporate neural collapse (NC) and align features to a fixed Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) as a uniform target for all classes. However, forcing tail classes to fully collapse over-contracts their samples and weakens generalization. To address this, we propose a controlled partial neural collapse, realized through two coordinated controls on a backbone: the Class-Adaptive Sparse Activation (CASA) classifier and the ETF-constrained adaptive margin (ETF-AM) loss. Rather than forcing a uniform full collapse, this regime allows head classes to collapse along the ETF while tail classes retain within-class diversity. This prevents the tail from being forced into full collapse, which is suboptimal under imbalance. To set the dimensionality of collapse, CASA induces class-related node specialization through feature-conditioned gating so that tail classes occupy their own feature directions. For the clearance axis, ETF-AM applies a frequency-adaptive margin, with smaller margins for head classes and larger for tail classes. On CIFAR100-LT, ImageNet-LT, Places-LT, and iNaturalist-2018, our method achieves the best overall accuracy over prior methods. In the empirical analysis, within-class spread increases monotonically from head to tail classes, consistent with tail classes retaining variability rather than fully collapsing.

b5474e95c5b8699f07ee94fe.title_original: What Should a Navigator Remember? Spatiotemporal Memory for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Navigation
b5474e95c5b8699f07ee94fe.excerpt: arXiv:2610.38318v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following a

86f793a1fe6638994e145e07.title_original: MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
86f793a1fe6638994e145e07.excerpt: arXiv:2610.38946v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Training-time multi-agent system (MAS) design seeks to learn reusable orchestration policies, yet prevailing approaches remain largely one-shot: an Orchestrator generates a system but only observes and learns from its terminal outcome. This paradigm discards execution trajectories that expose system-level failures and contain fine-grained information beyond the terminal outcome, leaving no direct basis for revising the source MAS, evaluating the updated MAS, or learning from the resulting contrast. To this end, we introduce MAS-Loop, an execution-grounded framework that closes this feedback loop by coupling an Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner. For each task, the Orchestrator constructs and executes a source MAS to obtain an outcome score and an intermediate trajectory. Conditioned on the trajectory, the Refiner localizes an actionable failure, formulates a trajectory-grounded diagnosis, and proposes a bounded patch to the agents, information flow, or execution configuration. The executable updated MAS is re-executed on the same task to measure its realized outcome under stochastic execution. This pair-MAS comparison provides complementary learning signals: the Orchestrator learns to generate strong systems with fewer recoverable failures, whereas the Refiner learns to expose and repair observed weaknesses, thereby driving policy-level co-evolution across training iterations. Experiments show that MAS-

9f93e96a53578ce534f454d2.title_original: Raincheck: Deferred Multimodal Prefill for Efficient Multi-Turn MLLM Inference
9f93e96a53578ce534f454d2.excerpt: arXiv:2610.39562v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-turn conversations with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reuse input context, but long multimodal inputs increase time to first token (TTFT). Query-aware hard pruning reduces prefill tokens but permanently excludes information that later questions may require. We propose Raincheck, a framework for deferred multimodal prefill that decouples initial token selection from later information availability. An existing pruning method selects tokens for initial prefill; Raincheck preserves and progressively prefills unselected tokens in source order using unused compute capacity during decode. Unfinished prefill continues after answer return during available scheduling gaps. Attention visibility control and affine state mapping enable context updates after generation begins in full-attention and hybrid recurrent models. Prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B with 30% initial multimodal-token retention. Across both models and four pruning methods, Raincheck recovers on average 77.7% and 60.4% of the quality lost to matched hard pruning on MultiVerse and ConvBench, respectively. On MultiVerse, the SGLang implementation reduces mean first-turn TTFT by up to 24.1% relative to full prefill, with less than 0.5% increase in mean time per output token (TPOT).

372ebff214d202131868935e.title_original: InterceptFuzz: Interception-based Stateful Fuzzing of Single-Process Targets
372ebff214d202131868935e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.03709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stateful protocol implementations are commonly fuzzed by tools that act as a network client and exchange messages with the target over sockets. Some wireless and IoT protocol stacks instead provide a single-process simulation platform, in which all nodes run in one binary and exchange packets in memory. Such simulations are deterministic and fast, which suits fuzzing, but offer no socket to which existing stateful fuzzers can attach. Meanwhile, fuzzing infrastructure such as Google's OSS-Fuzz supports only stateless engines. This paper presents InterceptFuzz, a middleware that enables stateful fuzzing of single-process targets on top of an unmodified stateless fuzzing engine. InterceptFuzz requires only a hook where the target passes packets between nodes. Through this hook, it records benign traffic and injects fuzzed packets. It organizes the observed packet sequences in a Prefix Tree. Each seed carries a State ID that selects a node of this tree, and InterceptFuzz deterministically replays the recorded prefix before delivering the mutated packet. The tree grows with newly discovered sequences, while redundant states are pruned to keep its growth in check. InterceptFuzz powered by AFL++ is evaluated on the Nexus test framework of OpenThread and on the LTE and Wi-Fi models of ns-3, against an interception-based adaptation of AFLNet and against Concat, an AFL++-based baseline that mutates a whole message sequence as one input.
