93499b1eeb0d8ddf03d2ff1a.title_original: Patients With Personality: Realistic Patient Simulation through Controlled Diversity and Selective Disclosure
93499b1eeb0d8ddf03d2ff1a.excerpt: arXiv:2606.17441v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Realistic patient simulation is a key requirement for developing and testing clinical LLMs at scale without costly user studies. Existing simulators lack realism and controllability: they overshare information and miss the variability of real patient behavior. Here, we introduce PatientsWithPersonality (PWP), a patient simulation framework that generates realistic yet diverse patient responses through explicit personality parametrization over a latent patient state. Grounded in the six-dimensional HEXACO personality model, it gives fine-grained control over conversational style, cooperativeness, and information disclosure. We evaluate PWP in the first direct comparison of different patient simulators under a shared protocol, anchored in transcripts of real physician-patient encounters. Clinicians judge PWP conversations as realistic at least as often as the recorded encounters themselves and far more often than prior simulators, and almost never flag them as "too informative". Our simulator also reproduces the disclosure pacing of real patients, and its HEXACO-conditioned personality traits can be recovered by clinicians and an autorater. PWP further shows a substantially wider behavioral range than the closest baseline. In a downstream benchmark, LLMs interviewing patients simulated by PWP perform closest to how they perform on the real encounters, whereas prior simulators make the task easier. PWP thus provides a rea

1a88f631a8ef9485eff900d6.title_original: Large-Language-Model Discovery of Quantum LDPC Codes through Structured Concept Evolution
1a88f631a8ef9485eff900d6.excerpt: arXiv:2606.24808v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check codes promise low-overhead error correction, but high-performing constructions remain hard to find. Here we introduce structured concept evolution, in which a large language model (LLM) evolves construction programs and their internal search strategies by modifying the finite group, protograph shapes or entry-assignment rule. We search for codes with fewer than $600$ data qubits and check weight at most $12$, optimizing $kd^2/n$ or the circuit-level logical error rate. Our method improves on published lifted-product benchmarks in selected parameter regimes, with exactly certified distances for the leading results. Circuit-level optimization typically yields lower logical error rates than $kd^2/n$ optimization, often despite smaller code distances. With the same evolution framework and step budget, the best LLM outperforms all random-mutation and hill-climbing runs on both objectives. Our results point to LLM-driven program search as an approach to designing general quantum LDPC codes.

cfc0251e672b1b15a1a0be02.title_original: Variable Bound Tightening for Nash Equilibrium Computation in Multiplayer Imperfect-Information Games
cfc0251e672b1b15a1a0be02.excerpt: arXiv:2606.25997v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: There has been significant recent progress in algorithms for approximation of Nash equilibrium in large two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games and exact computation of Nash equilibrium in multiplayer strategic-form games. While counterfactual regret minimization and fictitious play are scalable to large games and have convergence guarantees in two-player zero-sum games, they do not guarantee convergence to Nash equilibrium in multiplayer games. Recently, an approach has been presented for exact computation of Nash equilibrium in multiplayer imperfect-information games that solves a quadratically constrained program based on a nonlinear complementarity problem formulation derived from the sequence-form game representation. This formulation was solved using Gurobi's nonconvex quadratic solver, which employs spatial branch-and-bound to iteratively refine variable bounds by solving convex relaxations of bilinear terms. During presolve, Gurobi introduces auxiliary variables and, in some cases, binary variables, leading to an internal mixed-integer quadratically constrained program. This approach was demonstrated to outperform prior algorithms from the Gambit software suite and quickly solve three-player Kuhn poker after removal of dominated actions; however, the algorithm was not able to solve the full version of the game within 24 hours. In this paper, we derive finite bounds on slack and multiplier variables in t

599132f7e9f91cb7f4245c3e.title_original: Beyond the Prompt: Jailbreaking Function-Calling LLMs via Simulated Moderation Traces
599132f7e9f91cb7f4245c3e.excerpt: arXiv:2607.00481v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Jailbreak attacks remain a critical threat to the safe deployment of large language models (LLMs). While prior work has primarily studied attacks and defenses at the prompt level, we show that this prompt-centric paradigm overlooks a structural vulnerability in stateful, function-calling environments. In such applications, developer-defined schemas, structured arguments, and untrusted tool outputs are interleaved into a single shared model context. This architecture expands the attack surface by blurring the boundary between trusted control logic and untrusted data, allowing adversarial intent to be distributed across a multi-turn execution path. We exploit this architectural flaw through SMT, a black-box attack framework based on Simulated Moderation Traces. Departing from purely prompt-based interactions, SMT constructs a multi-turn trajectory that simulates a legitimate moderation-auditing workflow. Within this trajectory, a fabricated moderation frame leverages red-team testing as a pretext to elicit harmful generations. The subsequent validation feedback treats safety refusals as execution failures, prompting refinements that gradually weaken the model's safety constraints and ultimately trigger harmful outputs. Extensive empirical evaluations on prominent commercial LLMs from five different providers across two standardized safety benchmarks show that SMT consistently achieves the highest average attack success r

2d360c0bbc0ec7c6c1b60881.title_original: PixCon: Clean-Positive Contrastive Learning for Foundation-Model Semi-Supervised Segmentation
2d360c0bbc0ec7c6c1b60881.excerpt: arXiv:2607.03068v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Can a simple labeled-pixel contrastive branch improve semi-supervised segmentation with a strong pretrained encoder? We study this question with PixCon, which adds a class-wise memory bank to a DINOv2-Base implementation of UniMatch V2. The bank stores ground-truth-labeled features only where the student prediction agrees with the label. A multi-positive contrastive loss uses these features to train the shared encoder-decoder; the head and bank are discarded at inference. This simplifies earlier labeled-pixel banks by removing confidence thresholds and learned ranking. On Pascal VOC with 183 labels, PixCon improves all three paired seeds by 0.20, 0.64 and 1.83 mIoU points, raising the mean from 87.01 to 87.90. With 92 labels the mean gain is 0.40 points; single-seed differences on Cityscapes and ADE20K range from -0.08 to +0.14 points. A predicted-label contrastive control reaches nearly the same Pascal accuracy, so these results support the added branch rather than an accuracy benefit from its correctness filter. An exact gradient decomposition distinguishes mislabeled-positive counts from their similarity-weighted influence. Separate teacher diagnostics find retained-pixel error rates of 1.8% on Pascal and 10.6% on ADE20K. These diagnostics do not measure the training bank or predict final accuracy. 45610cbc6f8d9ba568093b7d.title_original: Hyperparameter Transfer in Graph Neural Networks
45610cbc6f8d9ba568093b7d.excerpt: arXiv:2607.05017v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The performance of deep learning models crucially depends on the settings of hyperparameters like learning rate, initialization scale, and weight decay. Hyperparameter transfer aims to make near-optimal hyperparameter settings consistent across model scale, so that large models can be optimized by proxy tuning their smaller, cheaper-to-optimize counterparts. While transfer principles are well-studied in the context of dense neural networks in language and vision tasks, they remain comparatively under-explored for graph neural networks (GNNs). We develop and validate a transfer parameterization for GNNs trained with SGD, Adam, and AdamW. Through theoretical scaling analyses and controlled experiments, we show that the proposed parameterization yields stable feature updates, learning rate transfer, and improved performance as width and depth increase. For SGD, we identify graph-dependent first-layer correction factors and show that their use can accelerate early training in graphs with sparse bag-of-words inputs. For Adam, we explore how different message passing normalizations affect early- and late-training transfer behavior, illustrating the importance of message passing normalization and advocating for an associated hyperparameter. For AdamW, we adapt a parameterization that allows for the joint transfer of weight decay and learning rate. Together, these results provide a practical recipe for scaling GNNs across a va

f698196797ff0b73f3b325be.title_original: GaP: A Graph-as-Policy Multi-Agent Self-Learning Harness For Variational Automation Tasks
f698196797ff0b73f3b325be.excerpt: arXiv:2607.05369v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For robots to work reliably in commercial and industrial applications, recent advances in agentic coding systems have potential to combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model-free policies. We focus on "Variational Automation" (VA), a class of tasks that have larger variations in object geometry and pose than fixed automation. Model-free policies often struggle to close the reliability gap for VA tasks, which must be executed persistently and reliably in commercial and industrial applications. Motivated by prior work on Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) and the Robot Operating System (ROS), we introduce Graph-as-Policy (GaP), a multi-agent coding harness that generates directed computation graphs with perception, planning, and control nodes from a Modular Open Robot Skill Library (MORSL). GaP generates an internal simulation environment to rehearse task instances with different graphs in parallel to iteratively refine the graph structure and parameters to improve success rates and throughput. Evaluation with 8 new open VA task benchmarks, 4 in simulation and 4 in real-world, suggests that GaP can achieve success rates that significantly outperform baselines. Details, code, and data: https://graph-robots.github.io/gap

5b8ef25409feb7c63c8dff7b.title_original: Token Time Continuous Diffusion for Language Modeling
5b8ef25409feb7c63c8dff7b.excerpt: arXiv:2607.14106v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper we introduce token time continuous diffusion (TTCD), a new diffusion language model which (a) operates in continuous space, deterministically mapping Gaussian noise to a final token canvas with no further sampling, and crucially (b) incorporates a new notion of per-token times, with some tokens proceeding from noise to token at a faster rate than others. Continuous space modeling helps TTCD avoid the parallel sampling of multiple tokens, which is a key source of inaccuracy at high speedups for models that iterate purely in discrete space. The notion of per-token times helps TTCD to better model conditional generation, allows for more sure tokens to proceed at a faster rate, and allows for differentiated inter-token influences during refinement. TTCD outperforms discrete models at high speedups. We train a 160M parameter TTCD model on OpenWebText, and then self-distill it; we find that at high speedups we are comparable in unconditional generation quality, and outperform in conditional generation, several existing models of similar size trained, on the same data, and self-distilled. We achieve similar gains in Sudoku solving as well.

24e757cef0e002d1ff1b1dd2.title_original: Revisiting data-driven dynamic security assessment with a tabular foundation model
24e757cef0e002d1ff1b1dd2.excerpt: arXiv:2607.16031v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Data-driven pre-fault dynamic security assessment (DSA) rapidly evaluates the dynamic risk of credible contingencies on a power system using machine learning (ML). Existing approaches face two limitations. First, they require a large labelled database for training, with a separate model trained, tuned, and maintained for each contingency in a potentially long list of credible contingencies. Second, the trained models generalize poorly to unseen contingencies. This work addresses these limitations by using a tabular foundation model (TFM) that assesses stability through in-context learning, and requires no retraining or hyperparameter optimization. We use a single TFM to assess many contingencies at once, removing the need to train one classifier per contingency. We also characterize when using electrical distance coordinates (EDC) as continuous features enables the TFM to generalize to unseen contingencies and when it does not, showing how a few labelled samples can reliably improve generalization. Through comprehensive case studies on the IEEE 68-bus system, we show that a single TFM attains an average Macro F1 score of about 90\% with only 120 labelled samples per contingency, outperforming both classical ML and deep learning baselines, without any model retraining or hyperparameter tuning. For held-out contingencies, we show that using just 10 labelled samples of the new contingency with a modified EDC encoding matc

f3a3ae8313918678df429452.title_original: Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training
f3a3ae8313918678df429452.excerpt: arXiv:2607.16097v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become central to improving large language models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, yet RL post-training is largely studied in isolation from the pretraining that precedes it. As a result, two basic questions remain open: (1) how do pretraining choices (model size, data) shape the returns to RL compute, and (2) what does RL actually do to the model? These questions are difficult to study in the standard LLM setting: pretraining corpora are vast and uncontrolled, making it hard to attribute behaviors to pretraining versus RL, and systematic compute sweeps across both stages are prohibitively expensive. To address these challenges, we use chess as a controlled testbed for studying reasoning across the full pretraining-to-post-training pipeline. We follow the standard LLM training pipeline by pretraining language models from 5M to 1B parameters on human chess games, supervised fine-tuning on synthetic reasoning traces, and running RL on chess puzzles with verifiable rewards. Using this framework, we find that the post-RL performance at given RL compute level is well-predicted from the pretraining loss, and slope of the RL reward curves improves approximately linearly with the pretraining tokens. Beyond scaling, we find that RL does not simply sharpen the SFT policy: on easy puzzles it amplifies correct moves the SFT policy already preferred, while on hard puzzles it surfaces correct moves

974dae26420dceecb33258c1.title_original: From Representations to Behaviors: Exploring the Person-Situation-Behavior Triad in LLMs
974dae26420dceecb33258c1.excerpt: arXiv:2607.26853v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Human personality theories characterize traits not as isolated attributes captured by a single score, but as stable individual tendencies expressed through the interplay among persons, situations, and behaviors. Existing studies of personality-related behavior in LLMs have primarily focused on outputs elicited under personality conditioning, characterizing observable trait-related expressions while lacking mechanistic evidence for the existence of internal personality-related representations, their cross-situational expression, and how these representations shape specific behaviors. Building on Funder's personality triad framework, we adapt its three components for LLM analysis: Person as personality-related internal representations, Situation as contexts that afford trait-relevant responses, and Behavior as response patterns on broader social tasks. We introduce a framework for discovering, controlling, and validating trait-like representations in LLMs. First, using contrastive behavior pairs grounded in shared situations, we identify sparse internal features associated with opposing poles of personality traits through SAE decomposition. We validate their trait relevance through effects on behavior to situation, token-level activation patterns, and robustness to paraphrasing. 1e665eb66c497879178b41c8.title_original: MD-ProTector: Positioning Multiple Data-Driven Prototypes for LLM-Generated Text Detection
1e665eb66c497879178b41c8.excerpt: arXiv:2608.10459v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As LLM-generated content becomes more sophisticated, detection systems for distinguishing those texts from human-written text must operate at scale while handling diverse writing styles, domains, languages, and generator models. Input-only encoder detectors are suitable for practical deployment setting, but standard binary classification supplies only the class label and does not explicitly organize the substantial variation within either class. We propose MD-ProTector, which represents each class with multiple trainable reference vectors in the encoder embedding space, referred to as prototypes. These prototypes provide separate decision boundaries for different groups of texts within the same class. However, adding multiple prototypes alone does not determine which variation each prototype should represent. MD-ProTector addresses this problem with Prototype Positioning loss, which separates class-level structure from the within-class variation that differentiates individual prototypes. Evaluated across five settings from three large-scale benchmarks covering domain, generator, language, and adversarial variation, MD-ProTector achieves the highest AvgRec on MAGE CDCM and RAID and the highest AUROC and lowest FPR95 on RAID among the compared encoder-based methods.

239be83d27f62075e64bb4bb.title_original: Fast and Memory-Efficient Wavelet Convolutions via I/O-Aware Reformulation
239be83d27f62075e64bb4bb.excerpt: arXiv:2608.10805v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Wavelet convolution (WTConv) has emerged as an increasingly popular drop-in replacement for standard convolutions, expanding a network's receptive field exponentially with the number of decomposition levels while keeping the parameter count linear. However, its reference implementation is severely memory-bound due to excessive data movement through high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We develop an I/O model of WTConv to characterize this bottleneck and use it to guide three algebraic reformulations: (1) recomputing the inexpensive Haar analysis butterfly on chip, (2) collapsing the multi-level synthesis cascade into a single closed-form pass indexed by output-coordinate bits, and (3) folding learned per-channel scales into the convolution weights. Together, these reformulations enable an I/O-aware fused implementation that substantially reduces HBM traffic. We evaluate the WTConvNeXt configuration across decomposition levels and a broad range of tensor shapes. Despite performing comparable arithmetic, the reference WTConv is substantially slower than the depthwise convolution it replaces. Our reformulation reduces modeled HBM traffic by approximately $2.55\times$, yielding up to a $4.35\times$ training speedup over the reference while roughly halving peak memory usage. b6504c96d98d87549d634fad.title_original: Trustworthy RAG: An Evaluation Agent for Detecting Misinformation and Knowledge Poisoning in Generative AI Systems
b6504c96d98d87549d634fad.excerpt: arXiv:2608.21095v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds Large Language Model (LLM) outputs in external knowledge, but RAG systems usually trust whatever they retrieve, creating a Security-Reliability Gap: high semantic relevance does not guarantee factual truth. Adversaries exploit this through knowledge poisoning, inserting malicious documents to cause targeted misinformation. We propose an Evaluation Agent, middleware that combines Natural Language Inference (NLI) factual verification, a five-signal poison detector with relevance-weighted aggregation, and a Trust Index T = 0.4 F + 0.35 C + 0.25 (1 - P ) with a non-linear dampener for high-contamination contexts. On TruthfulQA with Llama 3.3 70B, the agent reaches 91% accuracy and 100% precision, with 100% recall on instruction injection, while in-place edits, such as entity swaps, remain hard to detect. Across three LLMs the Trust Index stays discriminative, with a Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.73 to 0.81; generation style matters more than model size, and per-LLM threshold calibration restores baseline competitive accuracy, whereas a weaker FEVER result shows that cross-dataset generalization requires domain-specific calibration. 4a584fa7de3e6230642bcfcb.title_original: LongCounsel-8: A Benchmark Suite for Longitudinal Depression Tracking from Multi-Session Counseling Dialogues
4a584fa7de3e6230642bcfcb.excerpt: arXiv:2609.03507v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assess depression in counseling conversations, where psychology evidence suggests that tracking change across sessions matters more than any single score. However, existing dialogue benchmarks score each session on its own, and an accurate score for every session does not guarantee that a method follows the changes between sessions. We introduce LongCounsel-8, a benchmark for tracking depression across counseling sessions. Its systematic pipeline takes client profiles from real counseling cases, depression scores from real longitudinal data, and turn length and form from real counseling dialogues, yielding 7,749 five-session trajectories from three LLMs. Every session is generated to express a preset score on the PHQ-8, a standard eight-symptom depression questionnaire. Validation shows that the labels are self-consistent and the dialogues close to real counseling. Following clinical research on treatment monitoring, we propose a trend-based evaluation protocol reflecting real-world tracking needs: changes between sessions, crossings of the screening cutoff, trajectory types, and symptom-level changes. Extensive experiments show all five existing methods tested fall short in tracking trends: none estimates changes better than a no-change baseline, at most 40% of cutoff crossings are detected, and adding earlier sessions lowers change error but causes more missed imp

05f5959ccd6b2b46c682f70e.title_original: MAIA: Multi-Agent Intent Articulation for Requirement Discovery in Art Commissions
05f5959ccd6b2b46c682f70e.excerpt: arXiv:2609.12097v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In bespoke art commissions, laypeople know what they feel but lack the words to specify it: one participant wanted a laid-off truck driver depicted as "a ghost in his own machine" but left the medium, scale, and palette unsaid. We frame this as an articulation bottleneck at an under-served upstream stage: requirement discovery, which precedes any artist or image generator and forces the commissioner to constitute intent in the first place. We present MAIA (Multi-Agent Intent Articulation), a multi-agent system that scaffolds this stage through Socratic inquiry under a "Verification over Invention" rule, turning vague affect into a text-only brief of visual terms the user verifies. In a within-subjects study (N = 16), the full configuration produced a large, significant gain in Cognitive Support over a minimal baseline (r = 0.97, p_FDR = 0.003; LMM p_FDR < 0.001). Thematic analysis traces the same mechanism, and a validator gate structurally blocks unratified content. An exploratory blind review by three professional concept artists provides complementary descriptive evidence that the rewritten briefs were more complete and executable.

650afb673a7fdcad28cbb05a.title_original: PolicyMem: Geometric Policy Memory for LLM Governance
650afb673a7fdcad28cbb05a.excerpt: arXiv:2609.13734v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Effective LLM governance extends beyond detecting unsafe responses to guiding their correction through closed-loop assessment, revision, and verification. Learning-based guards provide strong semantic discrimination but often leave policy knowledge implicit in trained parameters, limiting its explicit reuse across stages. Programmable guardrails make policies explicit through prompts and workflows, but rely heavily on manual engineering to operationalize them. This motivates explicit policy representations that are both learnable and reusable across governance operations. To this end, we introduce PolicyMem, a geometric policy memory that compiles natural-language policies into learnable low-rank subspaces for reuse across governance stages. A policy assessor projects query-response representations onto these subspaces, producing evidence that directly mediates safety judgments and policy attribution. A response rewriter uses the implicated policies to revise unsafe responses, with the same assessor re-evaluating the revised responses. Beyond inference, the same memory constructs training data from model-generated candidates to supervise the rewriter without external teacher calls. Across five widely used benchmarks, PolicyMem achieves the best average unsafe-behavior detection performance among representative baselines while supporting effective policy attribution, rewriting, and post-intervention assessment through t

21f92c8f1d51de43bffc61b0.title_original: Decoupling Knowledge and Privacy: Post-Task Self-Distillation Replay for LLM Continual Learning
21f92c8f1d51de43bffc61b0.excerpt: arXiv:2609.29711v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Privacy-preserving continual learning (PPCL) must reduce the reproduction of sensitive content while retaining useful knowledge across sequential tasks. Formal privacy guarantees characterize randomized mechanisms, whereas operational output control concerns whether a trained model selectively reduces the likelihood of sensitive content in its outputs. In this work, we investigate the latter together with continual-learning utility under realistic task evolution. Retention and privacy correction operate at different granularities: task acquisition requires broad preservation of current- and old-task behavior, whereas privacy correction targets sparse annotated positions. Joint optimization leaves the current-task preservation target continually changing. We propose SPARK, a retention-correction decomposition that first freezes the learned post-task distribution and then applies selective correction around this stable reference. Self-Distillation Replay learns the current task while distilling behavior from previous tasks, and Post-Task Privacy Correction reduces annotated-PII likelihood while anchoring current- and old-task non-PII behavior to the resulting checkpoint. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that SPARK achieves effective selective PII suppression while preserving strong continual-learning utility and knowledge retention across diverse settings. Code and data will be released upon publication.

e653a7756cb9bb7409eca933.excerpt: arXiv:2609.34458v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Classical statistical theory is insufficient to explain the successes of general-purpose AI models, because it depends on handcrafted inductive biases that it cannot justify. No Free Lunch (NFL) theorems force any learner that beats chance on some environments to underperform on others. We might hope that past experience informs which environments to expect, but NFL applies equally to meta-learning. Thus, any method that makes meaningful predictions necessarily begins with an inductive bias external to the data. Choosing to bias toward short programs yields Solomonoff induction (SI), whose performance is competitive against all computable learners - albeit up to "constants" that become large when comparing against specialized methods that exploit background information. We therefore relativize SI to an information vantage point, biasing toward short programs with access to all preexisting information. This reframes the inductive bias: instead of seeking some absolute notion of simplicity, we favour accessibility with respect to our vantage point. An algorithm can only outpredict the relativized SI to the extent that its code contains additional information about the data, and no algorithm can generate such information. While SI is incomputable and hence not a practical algorithm, it provides a formal optimum for inference in the limit of infinite compute, and there is evidence to suggest that frontier AI systems roughl

b6895d56bd30607ea44e020a.title_original: Zero-Compute Cross-Lingual Transferability Estimation Using Typological Feature Proxies
b6895d56bd30607ea44e020a.excerpt: arXiv:2609.39640v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cross-lingual transfer describes how knowledge in a source language benefits a target language. Measuring it quantitatively requires broad multilingual pre-training, as prior work has done with cross-lingual transfer matrices. We ask whether transfer is predictable from freely available typological features, and whether the prominence of high-resource source languages reflects typology or data quality and quantity. We show that typological databases contain cheap and dense signals about cross-lingual transfer. Our typology-only random forest on a 24-language prior-work transfer matrix scores leave-one-language-out $\rho{=}0.705$ and $R^2{=}0.49$, against $\rho{=}0.62$ for a tuned non-typological control, an increment that a paired bootstrap cannot separate at this scale. When both languages of a held-out pair are unseen, performance degrades to $\rho{\approx}0.41$, so the model interpolates a ground-truth matrix more reliably than it predicts new languages. The signal survives leave-one-script-out and leave-one-family-out protocols, so script and family confounding do not explain the effect. By decomposing the transfer into a typology term and a resource-and-script bias term, we find the best-source ranking sensitive to this bias. Typological features never observe this bias, which makes them a zero-compute screening tool that replaces hundreds of training runs with a model fit. Our code is available \href{https://gith

eddf9b282ab9c1f064ac8261.title_original: SimForcing: Distilling Simulation Motion Priors into Real-Domain Robot World Models
eddf9b282ab9c1f064ac8261.excerpt: arXiv:2610.06598v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Action-conditioned robot world models must respond precisely to robot trajectories while preserving realistic visual dynamics, yet learning both from heterogeneous robot videos remains challenging. Simulation offers structured motion supervision, but appearance differences hinder direct transfer, and inaccurate simulation predictions can misguide real-video generation. We present SimForcing, a simulation-guided framework that uses simulation both as a source of transferable motion knowledge and as a controllable reference for prediction. First, we transfer motion knowledge from a simulation teacher through latent-motion distillation, aligning temporal changes in latent space to internalize motion priors while mitigating the influence of appearance differences. Second, we introduce multi-block simulation conditioning with condition dropout to exploit predicted simulation trajectories without relying excessively on their accuracy. Our simulation-conditioning classifier-free guidance scheme unifies these two ideas by balancing predictions based on internalized motion knowledge with those additionally guided by simulation latents. The jointly trained student generates both simulation conditions and real-domain videos, requiring no additional world model at inference. On Bridge, SimForcing achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD among the compared methods without external embodied pretraining. Evaluation on InternData-

6b06d702a1e712fd6e3218d2.title_original: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning
6b06d702a1e712fd6e3218d2.excerpt: arXiv:2610.16822v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. Neural architectures are operation-labeled directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where edge directions determine computational roles and execution dependencies. Existing graph Transformer predictors incorporate topological and directional information in different ways, but primarily focus on specific mechanisms rather than coordinated encoder-wide modeling of these semantics. We introduce encoder-wide directional consistency, a design principle that coordinates the modeling of directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature updates. To implement this principle, we propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer that integrates direction- and topology-aware node initialization, Magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative sequence-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and Magnetic spectral controls support the contribution of the direction-aware stages and orientation-sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics characterize module behav

35491f9e6c30ff11c4139055.title_original: Revisiting the 16x Pretraining Compute Gap between Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
35491f9e6c30ff11c4139055.excerpt: arXiv:2610.17590v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have attracted wide attention for their fast, parallel decoding, but they are believed to be far less efficient to train than autoregressive language models (ARMs): a widely cited study reports that a DLM needs roughly 16x the training compute of an ARM to match its likelihood, a figure that has made pretraining DLMs from scratch look prohibitive at scale. We find that the methodology behind this figure has fallen out of step with current DLM practice: it scores the model with its evidence lower bound (ELBO) and trains a full-sequence, decoder-only model. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of DLMs, adopting the exact likelihood under the model's own decoding order, block diffusion training, an encoder-decoder architecture, and a sweep over the block sizes used in practice. Under this new protocol, we study across ten model variants, about 1,700 models in total, and find that pretraining DLMs is far cheaper than previously thought. Concretely, scoring with the exact likelihood reduces the compute multiple to 12.8x; block diffusion training and an encoder-decoder architecture further reduce it to 7.8x at block size 32, and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6x at block size 8 and 3.0x at block size 4. We complement these scaling analyses with an empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder-decoder block diffusion, a held-out compute budget beyond the fitting range at which t

801f2852dd286cbbace57a4a.title_original: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
801f2852dd286cbbace57a4a.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21257v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bit-widths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weight and activation quantization, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning performance by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline, while maintaining performance close to the uniform integer baseline, with only a negligible 0.4%p degradation. These results hold across various configurations spanning seven models and

ae999c94abccd237ac1c8f82.title_original: X-Fly: Learning to Reach and Stop in Full-Chunk Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
ae999c94abccd237ac1c8f82.excerpt: arXiv:2610.21450v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) agents built on large vision-language models are expensive to query. Executing a complete predicted action chunk before replanning amortizes this cost, reducing model inference from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint for our policy. It also moves the states at which the policy is queried away from expert demonstrations, which supervise neither recovery from these states nor termination at the learner's own arrival. On OpenFly test-seen, no-stop failures account for 47.78% of full-chunk behavior cloning (BC) outcomes. We present X-Fly, a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial VLN. Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited decision states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in-region state. Flow-GRPO then jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from same-task closed-loop outcomes, supplemented by outcome-verified stopping supervision. With eight controls per decision, X-Fly reaches 74.18% SR on test-seen and 51.73% on test-unseen, compared with 16.45% and 18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04% and 29.46% for DreamFly.

f4a2932d4db0540dcbbd07c1.title_original: RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development
f4a2932d4db0540dcbbd07c1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.26826v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. We evaluate the resulting open-ended artifacts using independently verifiable keypoints and complementary programmatic and VLM judges. Across nine frontier (M)LLMs, the strongest system achieves an overall score of only 52.12 out of 100, revealing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains a substantial challenge for current models in practical webpage-development settings.

d0e9ba1323ebaa594162daf4.title_original: From Augmentation to Synthetic Evidence: Evaluating Generated Chest Radiographs at Dataset Intake
d0e9ba1323ebaa594162daf4.excerpt: arXiv:2610.29152v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While generated chest radiographs can serve as valuable data augmentation when explicitly declared, the same pixels become unsupported evidence when submitted as records of real clinical examinations. We study this dataset-intake vulnerability by disentangling three questions: (1) whether an image passes an automated technical quality check, (2) whether an origin classifier flags it as synthetic, and (3) whether a trusted provenance record supports the claimed clinical acquisition. In this study, a submitter uses Qwen3.8-27B to select up to 20 candidate radiographs from pools of 1,000 Cheff-identified or SynthCheX images, while a receiver evaluates image quality via MedGemma 1.5 and predicts origin using a linear probe over frozen DINOv3 features. Although quality selection increases MedGemma quality passes from 12/20 to 19/20 for Cheff-identified images and from 8/20 to 17/20 for SynthCheX, we find no evidence that candidate selection increases passage through both checks simultaneously: zero selected Cheff-identified images pass both gates, and uniform, quality-guided, and surrogate-guided selection yield 2, 1, and 2 SynthCheX passes out of 20, respectively. On unprocessed test cohorts, the origin classifier rejects 4,677 of 5,000 SynthCheX images at a nominal 5% false-alarm rate (flagging 110 of 2,297 real NIH radiographs), yet leaves 152 SynthCheX images that pass both pixel-level checks. b70c5b5ff685304ad83a5577.title_original: Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration
b70c5b5ff685304ad83a5577.excerpt: arXiv:2610.30105v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sequential decision-making under partial observability is difficult because agents must explore to infer hidden, task-relevant information before acting effectively. Learning such information-gathering behaviors tabula rasa via online reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient, whereas offline imitation averages expert actions across hidden states and fails to learn exploration. In this work, we propose ASTEROID, a simple and effective student--teacher supervised learning framework that can learn test-time exploration. Although a privileged expert never needs to explore, we demonstrate that a history-conditioned student can learn to do so when trained with on-policy contexts: the student first collects on-policy context under partial observability, and then imitates the privileged expert conditioned on that context. By distilling expert actions directly conditioned on the student's on-policy history, the student learns to systematically resolve partial observability, i.e., search while uncertain and exploit once the hidden state is revealed. This enables efficient test-time exploration (similar to Bayesian posterior sampling) without incurring the impractical training-data costs of reinforcement learning. Across a diverse range of eleven different environments, including discrete exploration benchmarks, robotic manipulation, navigation, and Procgen environments, ASTEROID achieves ~2x higher returns under fixed explor

284602274f934f5a6bdfa369.title_original: Bridging the Data Gap: Source-Informed Task-Space Transport for Few-Shot Diffusion
284602274f934f5a6bdfa369.excerpt: arXiv:2610.31323v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When an object category is well represented in one domain but scarcely observed in another, adapting a diffusion model to the target can be unreliable. Yet the same source-target relationship may have been observed for other categories. We ask whether this recurring relation can be learned and reused for a new semantic task. We introduce Meta-Diff, which embeds source and target distributions in a shared low-dimensional task space, learns an affine transport map across paired training tasks, and generates from the transported source coordinate using a shared diffusion backbone. At deployment, it requires source examples and the identity of a previously learned relation, but neither target images nor target-specific optimisation. Gaussian-mixture experiments examine how transfer depends on task information retained by the encoder, relation predictability and the size of the source--target shift. On held-out CIFAR-100 validation tasks, correct-source transport achieves 13.9% lower mean sliced Wasserstein distance than wrong-source transport. In the one-target final-test comparison, it achieves 14.7% lower mean distance than target-only adaptation and 32.7% lower than full fine-tuning under validation-selected settings. These gains have clear limits: directly applying the known corruption to clean-source generations performs better on CIFAR, and requested-class identity remains weak. Office-Home shows domain alignment wit

5f2c4819abf9b14b0ad24a24.title_original: SPARTA: A Sparse Ternary LLM Accelerator with Adaptive Attention and Unified Datapath for Long-Context Edge Inference
5f2c4819abf9b14b0ad24a24.excerpt: arXiv:2610.34824v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLMs on edge devices are constrained by limited memory and bandwidth. Although 1.58-bit ternary weights greatly reduce model storage, long-context inference is increasingly bottlenecked by KV-cache traffic and attention. Existing accelerators also use separate datapaths for ternary linear layers and attention, incurring hardware and execution overhead. We present SPARTA, a sparse ternary LLM accelerator for efficient long-context edge inference. SPARTA integrates: (1) a phase-aware sparse dataflow exploiting heterogeneous sparsity across compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode; (2) a unified compute fabric mapping ternary SpMM/SpMV and bit-serial attention onto shared processing elements to exploit zero-weight and zero-bit sparsity; and (3) an adaptive two-stage attention engine combining page-level Top-k selection to reduce K-cache accesses with token-level Top-p pruning to reduce V-cache traffic. SPARTA reduces KV traffic by 4.1-4.8x over full attention and 1.3-1.5x over a state-of-the-art sparse-attention scheme, with task-dependent quality loss. Compared with NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, SPARTA achieves 3.9x higher generation throughput and 8.3x higher end-to-end energy efficiency on average; versus AMD Ryzen 7 9700X, the gains are 5.0x and 81.7x. It also delivers 1.6-12.0x higher throughput, 2.0-4.2x higher energy efficiency, and 1.3-51.4x higher area efficiency than FIGLUT, TeLLMe, and MCBP.

053a44e9a244675875a0a286.title_original: Optimal Marginal Mixing for Transvection-Based Trapdoored Matrices over Large Fields
053a44e9a244675875a0a286.excerpt: arXiv:2611.05573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: \emph{Trapdoored matrices} are pseudorandom matrices admitting a fast matrix-vector multiplication algorithm given the secret key. We study a candidate family of such matrices: matrices generated by short random \emph{transvection walks} on \(\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\), whose steps are given by adding a random multiple of a random row of the current state to another. We show that the worst-case time for any nonempty set \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq [n]\times[n]\) of matrix entries to come within TV distance \(\varepsilon\leq \frac{1}{4}\) of its stationary marginal under this walk is \(\Theta(|\mathcal{S}|+n\log(n/\varepsilon))\), uniformly over all \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(q\geq Q_\mathrm{all}(n)\). This is asymptotically optimal, and resolves open questions about the mixing times of transvection walks. We derive concrete upper and lower bounds for \(n\geq 256\). Surprisingly, our bounds also hold conditioned on the row-pair structure of the walk, except on a fraction at most \(\varepsilon\) of such structures. This implies that these walks may be pseudorandom even after conditioning on the row-pair structure, and therefore that trapdoored matrices built with these walks may be universal. Assuming the conjectured structure-conditioned pseudorandomness of short walks, we exhibit highly efficient, highly parallelizable, and universal trapdoored matrices over \(\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\), \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\), and \(\mathb

e27f27ff977030b41492f68c.title_original: AQUA - A Modular Authentication Quality Modeling Framework
e27f27ff977030b41492f68c.excerpt: arXiv:2611.05660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Authentication solutions are the key design, architectural, and implementation decisions that implement authentication security controls. An example is a password-based authentication solution. While researchers often examine authentication quality, existing approaches do not distinguish which effects on quality stem from which aspect of authentication. For example, multi-factor authentication solutions tend to be less usable because they combine multiple authenticators, whereas passkeys are more secure than passwords because of properties inherent to the authenticator itself. This paper presents AQUA, a modular quality modeling framework for authentication solutions. AQUA's core idea is to decompose authentication into four interrelated concepts, enabling modular specification of authentication quality and tracing quality effects back to their source. We demonstrate AQUA with initial definitional quality models that address the levels of authenticators, authentication techniques, and authentication solutions. We further illustrate the interrelations between these concepts through concrete examples and a usability metric, showing how quality propagates across the concepts and ultimately affects the overall quality of an authentication solution. Our results provide a foundation for future work, including designing assessment and prediction models for authentication solutions and automated quality assessments.

9e5f191ce42f1fbd6da5c7af.title_original: Constraint-Aware Evaluation of Reinforcement Learning and Unsupervised Anomaly Detection for Security Operations Alert Triage
9e5f191ce42f1fbd6da5c7af.excerpt: arXiv:2611.05746v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) must identify real threats from large alert streams, but limited analyst capacity means that unnecessary escalations can delay more serious investigations. Existing studies often frame SOC alert triage as classification or anomaly detection, but both views are incomplete for production SOCs, where the central problem is selecting alerts worth escalating under limited capacity, asymmetric error costs, and workload constraints. This paper addresses that gap by formalizing alert triage as a constrained decision problem and evaluating three approaches: an offline reinforcement learning policy trained on alert embeddings, an Isolation Forest model built on operational features, and an autoencoder trained on historical benign alerts. These methods represent different triage assumptions: learning actions from reward, isolating unusual operational patterns, and detecting deviations from benign behavior. We evaluate all methods on 74,909 analyst-labeled production alerts under a strict temporal split and benign-escalation constraint. Because the test set contains 503 unique feature patterns, we primarily rank clusters of similar alerts. At the main operating point, all three methods satisfy the constraint, with the reinforcement learning policy achieving the lowest benign-escalation fraction at 0.000, compared with 0.007 for the autoencoder and 0.041 for Isolation Forest. The methods also prioritize lar

6621b0c20ac5aaeb553266ce.title_original: Private Vulnerability Testing for User Oversharing
6621b0c20ac5aaeb553266ce.excerpt: arXiv:2611.05779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Users can inadvertently increase their vulnerability to privacy attacks by oversharing personal information. In particular, the combination of individually innocuous attributes can place a user in a sufficiently small population to enable linkage or re-identification attacks. We present a privacy-preserving mechanism that allows users to determine whether the information they disclose places them below a predefined population threshold, without revealing their query or the data of other users. Our setting presents several practical challenges: users contributing data may be offline when queries are made, queries may select arbitrary subsets of attributes, and neither server should learn the queried population or its size. We address these challenges using secret-shared data and queries, private equality testing, and secure threshold computation. Our protocol provides computational privacy against a malicious client and semi-honest, non-colluding servers, while supporting arbitrary queries and dynamic database updates. We define reactive $f$-privacy for a dynamically evolving database and prove that our construction satisfies it, with the sequence of permitted threshold outputs defining the information available to the adversary across an execution. We optimise the protocol using oblivious-transfer extensions and pre-computation, achieving sub-second online query times for 96-bit queries on datasets of up to one million records.

c997069cde5aca8732a8cd17.title_original: Timing is Everything: Inferring Temporal Membership in Continually Updated Models
c997069cde5aca8732a8cd17.excerpt: arXiv:2611.05781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual model updating has become a common practice in the deployment of machine learning systems. However, the dynamic training behaviors give rise to new risks not sufficiently addressed by existing studies. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of temporal privacy risk in continually updated deep learning models. We formalize the notion of temporal membership in continually updated models. We then define the temporal membership inference attack, which seeks to infer whether and when individual samples were involved in model training, at both timestamp-level and interval-level granularities. To this end, we propose TMIA, a novel black-box attack that leverages bidirectional LSTMs to infer temporal membership from model outputs observed across successive updates. Through extensive experiments on three language models and three image classification models, we show that TMIA is highly effective and significantly outperforms existing baselines. Finally, we evaluate three potential defenses, revealing the trade-off between privacy protection and model utility.

25bb222cf8bff73c03aba407.title_original: GRIDSHIELD: Verifiable Grid Feasibility and Manipulation Resistance in Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading
25bb222cf8bff73c03aba407.excerpt: arXiv:2611.05816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blockchain-based peer-to-peer (P2P) energy markets let neighbors trade directly, but concentrate unchecked power in the clearing operator. Most prior work addresses only part of this: network-aware clearing respects grid constraints but operates on plaintext allocations, while privacy-preserving designs hide bids yet either drop the network constraint, enforce it only inside an unauditable computation, or recover it at the cost of a per-circuit trusted setup. Neither considers what happens if an adversary captures the operator's clearing privilege to reorder trades for profit or curtail a rival. We present GRIDSHIELD, a P2P energy-trading system that clears sealed bids with an order-independent batch program, removing the welfare a compromised operator can extract by reordering trades, and proves the result grid-feasible via an aggregated congestion-feasibility proof (ACFP). Exploiting the additive homomorphism of Pedersen commitments, ACFP reconstructs each grid constraint directly from per-bus commitments, reducing feeder-wide feasibility verification over any public grid constraints to a single aggregated range proof over the hidden allocation, with a reveal-and-recompute challenge that catches feasible yet unfair clearings. We introduce congestion-responsibility fairness (CRF), a metric scoring curtailment against each party's physical responsibility for congestion rather than consumption. We evaluate GRIDSHIELD against thre

2af3f9af164c205305961b70.title_original: Enforcing Accountable Disclosure in Confidential AI
2af3f9af164c205305961b70.excerpt: arXiv:2611.05971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in CPU and GPU confidential computing enable confidential AI, allowing LLMs to process user prompts without exposing them to service providers or infrastructure operators. However, AI agents often need to send prompt-derived information to external services, and providers may also require limited disclosure for safety monitoring and failure diagnosis. We propose CORDE, a system for confidential virtual machines (CVMs) designed to satisfy the principle of Confine or Declare: user-derived data is confined by default, but when necessary, it may leave the CVM only after being "declared." To "declare" data is to record its exact contents, recipient, and stated reason in a user-accessible, tamper-evident declaration log. To put this principle into practice, we present an integrated system design that combines per-user information-flow control in Rust with a TEE-based ledger and remote attestation. Our evaluation on an NVIDIA H100 GPU shows that declaration before disclosure adds little overhead in task latency, about 0.5% on the AppWorld agent benchmark. CORDE provides a basis for accountable disclosure of user data, supporting responsible and transparent data management in AI services.

4184feab8a8c0ee7e9eddbdc.title_original: CoordX Protocol: Peer to Peer Cryptographically Verified Shared Records
4184feab8a8c0ee7e9eddbdc.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People, companies and software agents often must work on shared records even when they do not trust each other. Today they usually give those records to a central server. The server keeps the canonical copy, authenticates users, and decides who has permissions to act on the record. The CoordX Protocol removes the need for that central server. In the CoordX protocol the author of a record holds full permission over it. Permission for any other party to create, read or update the record is assigned by explicit grants and keys. An invitation only starts contact between two parties. It gives no permission. Each record is a causal tree of signed entries, and each entry is immutable. Each entry names the permission that allowed it. Any party can get the proof of that permission and check it without help from anyone. Two honest parties that check the same bytes, with the same keys and local settings, always get the same answer. The content is encrypted, so the relays that may carry it in transit see only sealed bytes. To exclude a party from future content, the other parties move to new keys. The protocol does not choose a winning version, does not put entries in time order, and does not need global agreement. Applications decide what the entries mean above the level of the protocol.

1d48767a61e757d3f44f42a5.title_original: PIMROP: A Feasibility Study of Return-Oriented Programming on Commercial Processing-in-Memory Architectures
1d48767a61e757d3f44f42a5.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Processing-in-Memory places small programmable cores on the memory device, where they execute beside the DRAM banks and beyond the control-flow defenses that protect host programs. The security of this in-memory code is an attack surface that remains largely unstudied. We present PIMROP, to our knowledge the first demonstrated code-reuse attack on a commercial Processing in-Memory ISA. We show that return-oriented programming is feasible on a real, commercially shipped PIM instruction set, the UPMEM DPU, whose DRAM Processing Units run C compiled by a dedicated LLVM toolchain. We build Galileo-for-DPU, a gadget scanner adapted to the DPU's fixed-width, 8-byte-aligned RISC encoding, and run it entirely on the UPMEM functional simulator in a reproducible Docker and VM environment. We find the runtime library that every kernel links already yields 517 non-trivial gadgets covering all five canonical ROP primitive classes, and all 13 PrIM benchmarks we scanned carry gadgets as well. We then demonstrate two verified end-to-end attacks, each reproducible on 10 of 10 runs. In the first, a stack buffer overflow in a DPU kernel overwrites the saved return address and diverts control into a routine that copies a secret into host-readable memory. In the second, we leak the same secret using a chain of reused gadgets alone, without diverting control into any such routine. We further show that two standard defenses--stack canaries and _FORTIF

f848012b9aad51bb7a66a4f8.title_original: Securing Web Agents with the Compile-Then-Execute Paradigm
f848012b9aad51bb7a66a4f8.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web agents commonly follow the ReAct paradigm, selecting each action from runtime observations that inherently mix trusted and untrusted content. This design makes their control flow vulnerable to prompt injections embedded in webpages. We introduce Baya, a compile-then-execute web agent designed to prevent prompt-injection-driven control-flow hijacking by design. Before accessing the live website, Baya compiles the user's request into an executable Python program that calls a Trusted Website API. The planning model does not observe live website content; only the compiled program processes it. Untrusted data may determine program values or select among branches defined during compilation, but it cannot redefine the user task or cause the model to synthesize new website operations at runtime. The Trusted Website API gives the compiler a unified view of the website's action space, enabling ahead-of-time planning without the stepwise action discovery required by reactive agents. Our evaluation across 581 valid WebArena Verified tasks shows that Baya achieves 77.8% aggregate utility, outperforming browser-only ReAct (55.1%) and API-enabled ReAct (66.7%). On WASP, a security benchmark for web agents, Baya achieves 0% attack success rate, compared with 16.2% for API-enabled ReAct and 25.5% for browser-only ReAct.

cd04bb8940197785c8a54320.title_original: SenTrojan: Revealing Analog Hardware Trojan Attacks on Sensors
cd04bb8940197785c8a54320.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sensors bridge the physical and digital worlds, making their integrity critical to cyber-physical system security. Existing sensor attacks largely exploit unintended and sensor-specific physical vulnerabilities, limiting their generalizability and motivating a different threat model, i.e., whether an adversary can implant hidden attack surfaces into sensors before deployment. In this paper, we present SenTrojan, an analog hardware Trojan framework for sensors. SenTrojan embeds malicious functionality into analog signal circuitry commonly shared across diverse sensor architectures, and activates the hidden behavior through crafted external physical signals. Once activated, SenTrojan can induce sensor malfunctions ranging from permanent denial-of-service to static or dynamic spoofing. To achieve these effects under different architectural constraints, we introduce two complementary designs. The Logic-Rule-Driven (LRD) Trojan adds lightweight analog monitoring logic to detect trigger features such as frequency and amplitude, enabling reliable activation across various sensor types. The Physical-Effect-Driven (PED) Trojan targets sensors with exploitable native analog effects, e.g., nonlinearity and rectification, and realizes attacks with minimal component insertion. We evaluate SenTrojan on 14 sensors spanning 6 transduction principles and demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse real-world scenarios. Overall, SenTrojan achiev

4f31d985088a16fa8af7aa62.title_original: KVGuard: A KV Cache Safety Checker for LLM Serving Systems
4f31d985088a16fa8af7aa62.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern LLM serving systems manage the KV cache through PagedAttention, a custom GPU allocator that partitions a single CUDA-allocated region into fixed-size physical blocks and maps each request to those blocks through a CPU-built block table. This block-based design exposes a previously unstudied class of memory safety bugs in the KV cache, including double-free, use-after-free, out-of-bounds access, uninitialized read, and permission violation, which silently corrupt outputs or break request isolation without ever crashing the system. Existing memory sanitizers cannot detect them, because they reason about CUDA-level addresses rather than KV cache blocks, requests, and block tables, and their redzone- and quarantine-based designs do not fit the scarce GPU memory budget of LLM serving. This paper presents KVGuard, the first systematic memory-safety abstraction for KV cache management in LLM serving systems. KVGuard maintains a compact shadow block for each physical KV block, recording per-request permission and per-entry initialization, and uses this metadata to perform five safety checks across the PagedAttention workflow, spanning CPU allocation, block table construction and translation, and GPU-side block table lookup and KV entry access. Each check fires at the boundary that introduced the violation, enabling early detection during development rather than reporting downstream output corruption many requests later. A prototy

0a2d9a5a169214554656d67b.title_original: Network Intrusion Forensic Detection System with Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Digital Chain of Custody
0a2d9a5a169214554656d67b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deploying an explainable intrusion detection model from a validated laboratory setting into a forensic workflow requires guarantees that benchmarks do not test: that the certified model is the exact artifact applied to a case, that heterogeneous evidence can be classified reliably, and that every step is verifiable. We present MODEXRE, a forensic pipeline that extends a previously validated synthetic-data-trained XGBoost classifier with SHAP explainability (arXiv:2607.00763) into a dual-mode architecture: a Laboratory mode, where models are trained and certified on public and synthetic data, and a Formal mode, where a frozen, hash-verified model performs inference on case evidence under a SHA-256 hash-chained chain of custody. Suricata alerts, CEF firewall logs and packet captures are normalized through OCSF. After correction, the same capture went from 100% of events flagged as malicious to 87% classified as Normal, with the scanning host

b7832c9bf15b0160094485a7.title_original: Beyond the Landing Page: Website Blocking, Tracker Visibility, and Human Alignment in Automated Web Crawls
b7832c9bf15b0160094485a7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web tracking studies largely rely on automated crawlers, yet their measurements can differ from what people encounter while browsing. Conventional crawlers follow predefined navigation rules, whereas LLM-driven agents decide how to navigate and interact with websites, potentially changing the tracking they encounter. We compare agentic and non-agentic crawlers to examine how websites respond to them, what tracking they record, and how closely their observations match human browsing. Across 2,000 popular websites, we evaluate different navigation strategies, automation frameworks, and stealth configurations, alongside browsing data from 26 participants. We find that website denials increase beyond landing pages for standard browser automation, while a detection-resistant automation framework largely prevents this escalation without increasing recorded tracking. On the same URLs, agentic crawlers record tracking activity from 1.5-1.7 times as many third-party organizations, particularly on consent-managed pages. Agentic crawlers recover 82-87% of tracker organizations observed by participants, compared with 58-68% for non-agentic crawlers, yet roughly half of their own observations are absent from human participant visits. These findings show that avoiding website interventions, increasing tracking visibility, and achieving closer agreement with human observations do not necessarily go hand in hand, highlighting the need to select

17e459f626db251bd51d9ee3.title_original: Explainable Anomaly Detection in 5G Networks through Continuous Time Graphs
17e459f626db251bd51d9ee3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: 5G networks increasingly resemble distributed systems in their design. It then becomes crucial to move beyond traditional network-based detection methods and to explore alternative approaches. In this work, we propose a formalization of 5G network exchanges as a dynamic graph, on which we apply techniques from the field of graph-based learning to detect anomalies effectively. This representation allows for fine-grained analysis of packet-level semantic content, while simultaneously capturing sequential and topological contexts, both of which are essential for identifying sophisticated and multi-stage attacks. To assess the effectiveness of this formalism, we evaluate it with the most popular dynamic graph models, demonstrating its potential for 5G anomaly detection.

b2d4b5be09fc9af49039c06d.title_original: Analysis of Local Open-Weight LLM Agents on Vulnerability-Reproduction Tasks
b2d4b5be09fc9af49039c06d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight language models that fit on a single consumer GPU are becoming capable on a growing range of tasks, and they matter because they can run locally without sending the code to a hosted service. Vulnerability reproduction, turning a vulnerability description into an input that crashes the vulnerable build, is a natural target for them, since it is an automated analysis task closer to test generation than to code comprehension and it runs against a build that must be executed rather than read. In order to assess whether current models can perform it, we evaluate twelve configurations of local models, spanning three generations, two architectures and three quantization levels, on ten CyberGym vulnerability-reproduction tasks, three runs each under one harness, and release the full artefact. We show that every configuration, down to the 4B model, solves most of the six easier tasks, and configurations separate only on the remaining four. For the harder tasks, the 27B model is required. Quantization did not change what the models solved in any matched pair, but it changed how fast they got there, and the mixture of experts reached the same scores in less wall clock. We also examine the agent trajectories. Almost every run we examined, including those that fail, names the vulnerable function and states the correct hypothesis, and what separates a solved task from an unsolved one is whether that hypothesis becomes a working in

b3fcb5777a0d9ac4f84a1c48.title_original: Beyond Identity Creation: Bilinear Sybil Cost in Identities and Time
b3fcb5777a0d9ac4f84a1c48.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sybil defenses price the creation of an identity, yet influence goes, again and again, to active identities. We study the cost of maintaining influence. A defense has a bilinear Sybil cost with ratio $A$ if keeping $s$ identities active for $T$ periods costs at least $sT/A$ honest units: the average cost per identity-window is at least $1/A$ times an honest participant's cost. Recurrence alone does not guarantee this cost. The cost can be carried over from earlier periods, shared among many identities, or be negligible when fast hardware does the work of thousands of honest devices. We give four sufficient conditions for a defense that checks every identity each period to achieve bilinear Sybil cost: identity binding, freshness, a shared deadline, and sequential, non-batchable work. They yield two guarantees: a bilinear total cost, with $A$ the speed advantage of the adversary's fastest hardware, and, because the work must be fresh and finished by a common deadline, a bound on the identities active in a period by the processors running at that time. We prove that none of the four follows from the other three. A verifiable delay function on an identity-bound input meets all four without payments, with $A$ of 2 to 8 for CPUs and about 28 for a hypothetical ASIC, against $10^3$ to $10^7$ for hash puzzles. We measure one active identity per core per period against about 80,000 under a signed heartbeat, no gain from batching up to 1,

a7e61b3b7b7bb3100efb353c.title_original: Clear Human Web: Where a Person Vouches for Every Client
a7e61b3b7b7bb3100efb353c.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The web cannot tell whether a request comes from a person or from a program. Sites have checked the network address and puzzles in its place, and both have given way: automated traffic exceeds human traffic, and puzzles are solved for pay and by agents. This paper proposes the Clear Human Web, the part of the public web that sites open only to clients a person vouches for. A person's wallet presents their person identification data (PID) to one issuer, the only party that registers as a relying party, and receives a bounded number of blind-signed tokens, proofs of personhood that carry no attribute. The browser spends one token at each site that runs the gate, and the site learns that a valid token of a trusted issuer was spent, and nothing else. No field is added to the PID, no protocol is introduced, no site registers, and the publisher of a site holds the same proof as its readers. We define the Clear Human Web through five properties and seven adversaries, and state which properties the construction satisfies against each adversary. The identities a person can hold on one site in an epoch are bounded to k. The bound holds once the wallet limits a person to one pseudonym at the issuer. In the optimum k = 1, and a zero-knowledge proof of PID possession and a pseudonym per site replace the tokens.

55676ee473f786170b569dd4.title_original: CoRTeC: A Differentially Private Release for Synthetic Tabular Data, Decodable by Any Generator
55676ee473f786170b569dd4.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The records that could train the most useful models, such as a hospital's patient files, are often the ones an institution cannot share. We propose CoRTeC, a method that releases synthetic versions of such records under differential privacy. Differential privacy places a proven limit on what the synthetic data can reveal about any person, and in particular on membership inference. CoRTeC spends the privacy budget once, on a small file of noisy counts designed for training a classifier. For each group of records, the file gives the group's size, its balance of outcomes, a histogram of every column for each outcome and the outcome rate in each of several non-overlapping cells. A reviewer can check every number before the file leaves the institution. Anyone can then turn the counts into synthetic rows, as often as they like and at no further privacy cost. A maximum-entropy decoder can do this without any language model, and so can each of the five frozen language models we tested. None of them ever sees a real record. A selection step then matches the rows to the released counts. Decoded without a language model, the automatically configured release at $\varepsilon = 2$ trains classifiers to within 0.02 AUC of a real sample of the same size on the Adult dataset, across three data splits. On NHANES and bank marketing, without the selection step, it stays within 0.05 AUC. On Adult, with a fixed cohort rule, the release carries the ou

50e96e0514656f167392587d.title_original: Shoot on (Core)Sight: Re-enabling Secure Debug on the RP2350 with Photon-Emission Microscopy and Laser Fault Injection
50e96e0514656f167392587d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-resistant policy storage does not guarantee fault-resistant enforcement. We demonstrated this distinction on the RP2350A4 using differential photon-emission microscopy (PEM) and laser fault injection (LFI). PEM narrowed the area for laser scanning, which found two sites where pulses set the DEBUGEN bits enabling core~1 Secure debug. An online attack sequence using only Serial Wire Debug (SWD) feedback restored sustained access. After rescue reset, the sequence recovered a 128-bit test secret. This reset reloads the secret's runtime page lock from a stored policy that permits Secure reads and prevents user firmware from tightening the lock.

92cbf374c8b9473658f70c8f.title_original: Towards Early Warning of Real-World Vulnerabilities: An Evidence-Aware Decoupled Method for CVSS Vector Prediction Based on Unstructured Disclosures
92cbf374c8b9473658f70c8f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.06477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Early assessment of Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) vectors from Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) can reduce the delay between initial public disclosure and official National Vulnerability Database (NVD) scoring. Existing predictors, trained mainly on standardized late-stage descriptions, degrade on noisy and incomplete pre-NVD reports. We introduce PARSE, a vulnerability-disclosure lifecycle model, and VPre, an early assessment framework built on two-level Evidence-Aware Decoupling. Decoupling Level I, Security-Evidence Screening, separates security-relevant evidence from noisy early reports at the report and sentence levels. Decoupling Level II, Evidence-Matched Routing, decouples the prediction task of the eight CVSS metrics into a scattered-evidence class and an explicit-evidence class based on validation-set measurements, matching each with a targeted predictor: large-language-model reasoning for the former, lightweight supervised classification for the latter. On the 851-report held-out test split of the 5,581-report VPre-Bench, VPre achieves a mean absolute error of 0.7239 -- 44.7% below the reproduced BERT-Small-NVD early-transfer baseline; paired timestamps across the full benchmark show an average 38-day lead before official scoring (observed range 21-60 days).
